articles.title: Pro-life CEO predicts Trump FDA nominee could bring renewed scrutiny to abortion drug risks
articles.summary: Trump's FDA nominee Heidi Overton could bring renewed scrutiny to mifepristone, says Americans United for Life CEO who calls her a "pro-life" pick.
articles.body: The chief executive of America's oldest pro-life organization told Fox News Digital that President Donald Trump's FDA nominee, Dr. Heidi Overton, could bring renewed scrutiny to mifepristone, the abortion drug at the center of an ongoing federal safety review. John Mize, CEO of Americans United for Life (AUL), said he has had five or six conversations with Overton, who is known for her pro-life views. She currently serves as Trump's deputy assistant for domestic policy. "I think she's going to bring objectivity to the issue of mifepristone in a way that will expose this drug for the damage it causes women," Mize said in an interview on Friday, adding that his organization is "optimistic" that Overton will be a "pro-life FDA commissioner." Overton's nomination comes just weeks after an 18-year-old woman in North Carolina was accused of using mifepristone and misoprostol to terminate a pregnancy at 31 weeks, well beyond mifepristone's FDA-approved limit of 10 weeks. HAWLEY INTRODUCES BILL TO STRIP FDA APPROVAL FROM 'INHERENTLY DANGEROUS' ABORTION PILL Mize has led AUL for two-and-a-half years, but the nonprofit has advocated against abortion, euthanasia, assisted suicide and other practices it considers threats to human life since its founding in 1971. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 1-800-273-TALK (8255). Mize said he believes Overton is the "right candidate" to lead the FDA, citing her experience in government, clinical medicine and medical research. If confirmed, Overton would take the reins of the agency responsible for regulating abortion medication, including mifepristone. Mifepristone carries an FDA boxed warning, the agency’s strongest safety warning, for the risk of serious and sometimes fatal infections or bleeding. Prompted initially by COVID-19 pandemic restrictions, the FDA stopped enforcing the drug's in-person dispensing requirement in 2021 and later removed it permanently after reviewing the available safety data. Under current FDA rules, patients do not necessarily have to see a physician in person before receiving a prescription, allowing mifepristone to be prescribed after telehealth visit and mailed by a certified pharmacy. Mize wants those rules tightened. SUPREME COURT TEMPORARILY BLOCKS APPEALS COURT RULING ON ABORTION PILL, RESTORES WIDER ACCESS TO DRUG "Dr. Overton and I share a very similar perspective that the drug is dangerous, particularly in an unregulated way for women," Mize told Fox News Digital. "I firmly believe she understands the clinical implications of taking a drug with a black box warning and now shipping it in the mail." Overton has publicly criticized mifepristone and other abortion drugs, which accounted for about 65% of clinician-provided abortions in 2023, according to the Guttmacher Institute, up from 53% in 2020 before the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade. In a February 2023 policy brief for the America First Policy Institute, a MAGA-aligned think tank where she previously served as chief policy officer, Overton denounced federal policymakers for expanding access to abortion pills. She also accused the Biden administration of using the COVID-19 pandemic to wrongly justify allowing mifepristone and misoprostol, a drug that induces early labor, to be sent to patients through the mail. FIRST ON FOX: TOP REPUBLICANS TAKE ABORTION PILL FIGHT TO SUPREME COURT, CITING COERCION AND SAFETY RISKS Taken together, the two drugs terminate early pregnancies: mifepristone blocks progesterone, a hormone needed to sustain the pregnancy, while misoprostol causes contractions that expel the fetus. "Abortion is corrosive to children, women, and society broadly because it devalues and extinguishes innocent human life," she wrote at the time. "America First policies should focus on immediately halting the effort to normalize abortion-on-demand and on broadly recognizing the evidence of the risk posed to women." Mize pointed to a 2025 study by the Ethics and Public Policy Center, a conservative think tank, that analyzed insurance claims from 865,727 mifepristone abortions between 2017 and 2023 and found a serious adverse event rate of nearly 11%. This included conditions such as hemorrhaging, sepsis or infection. The study received immediate pushback, with the medical community saying it used a flawed methodology. The paper was also not peer-reviewed or published in a medical journal, factors Mize said Overton is aware of. HAWLEY SENDS CRIMINAL REFERRAL OF 'LEFT-WING DARK-MONEY' GROUP OVER MAILED ABORTION DRUGS "It's not the whole picture, and Dr. Overton would say that," Mize said. "But it's an important indicator as to what's happening in the real world. So I believe she will do a really good job of evaluating the study." Mize said he hopes Overton will impose tighter restrictions on mifepristone after reviewing the evidence, potentially restoring a requirement that women see a doctor in person before receiving a prescription. He described Overton as "measured" and "methodical" while cautioning that pro-life advocates should not expect her to pursue immediate, sweeping changes at the FDA. "I don't get the sense that she's gonna move quickly on issues," Mize said. SUPREME COURT KEEPS BROADER ACCESS TO ABORTION PILL MIFEPRISTONE IN PLACE WHILE LEGAL FIGHT CONTINUES Dr. Marty Makary, the previous FDA commissioner, resigned in May after clashing with Trump administration officials and Republican lawmakers. He also drew criticism from pro-life activists, who accused the agency under his leadership of slow-walking its safety review of mifepristone. If confirmed, Overton would inherit the review, which was formally announced in September 2025 and does not have a scheduled completion date. The FDA has noted these types of studies typically take a year or longer to conduct. After that review is completed, Mize said the next step for Overton, ideally, would be "a longer term, deep dive evaluation on this medication to determine if it should even be on the market." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Mize acknowledged that not all the evidence is in yet but made clear that his preference would be to take mifepristone off the market. "From my perspective, any medication that denies someone the opportunity to live and kills a human being shouldn't be something that we're promoting amongst the FDA," Mize said. "Ultimately, I would love to see this drug removed from the market for those reasons. Culturally, we might not be there right now." Overton’s confirmation hearing has not yet been scheduled but is expected to take place after the Senate returns from its summer recess on Sept. 14.

articles.title: Places that have been renamed during Trump’s second term
articles.summary: President Trump said renaming Lake Ontario is under “serious consideration.” It wouldn’t be the first place renamed during his second term.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – Amid the ongoing trade war with Canada , President Trump said Tuesday that renaming Lake Ontario as “Lake America” is under “serious consideration.”

Trump didn’t give many details in a Truth Social post , but explained that the U.S. doesn’t “expect to be doing much business with Ontario any longer.”

While Ontario Premier Doug Ford dismissed the idea , calling it “a lot of rhetoric” while speaking to CNN, the Great Lake would not be the first site to be renamed since Trump took office for a second time.

After taking office in January 2025, Trump signed orders to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America, and Mount Denali as Mount McKinley .

In February, North Carolina military base Fort Liberty was reverted back to Fort Bragg . The base had been known as Fort Liberty since 2023, when Congress, as part of a congressionally mandated rule to rename installations honoring Confederate generals, changed it.

Back in December, the Trump administration changed the name of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory to the National Laboratory of the Rockies .

Trump has also called for other things outside his purview to be renamed, like reverting the name of the Washington Commanders back to a dictionary definition of a slur against Native Americans.

Trump’s name, signature, and likeness have also found their way onto several other places during his second term. That includes “limited edition” passports , National Park Service passes , and currency .

His name has also been added to the Kennedy Center and the U.S. Institute of Peace building, and Florida’s Palm Beach International Airport has adopted the name “President Donald J. Trump International Airport.”

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trump administration says it might demolish the Kennedy Center if court blocks renovations
articles.summary: Justice Department attorneys called the Kennedy Center “structurally unsound, fundamentally unsafe, and embarrassing to the Nation’s Capital.”
articles.body: The Trump administration is, for the first time, threatening the demolition of the Kennedy Center if the arts institution isn’t allowed to follow its plans for the site, including adding President Donald Trump’s name to the front of the building. “Without those efforts, the Center will deteriorate further into an unsafe, decrepit structure that will be required to be taken down, with a determination to follow on what to build on the site, such as a large outdoor amphitheater overlooking the Potomac River that has been proposed, by some, for many years,” Justice Department attorney Brantley T. Mayers wrote in a court filing on Monday. The filing notes that any potential outdoor amphitheater would “fail to adequately honor” President John F. Kennedy, “but would be simpler and more economical to build, operate, and maintain.” The DOJ attorneys called the Kennedy Center “structurally unsound, fundamentally unsafe, and embarrassing to the Nation’s Capital.” They said the center’s board, which was handpicked by self-appointed chairman Trump, “recognizes that President Trump’s efforts and prestige provide the sole hope for the Center’s financial survival, and structural renewal.” “The Board also underscores, and the undisputed evidence demonstrates, that without the prominent recognition of The Trump Administration, and President Trump’s efforts, the donors will not contribute, and the Center will continue to be in a financial and structural death spiral. The Trump Administration, and President Donald J. Trump, should, therefore, be given the respect and dignity of acknowledgement,” the filing says. It notes that Trump “obtained $258 million in funding from Congress for capital restoration, and has marshalled a new donor base to finance an endowment for the Center,” but does not say what has happened to that money. The filing makes a dramatic twist in the monthslong saga to renovate the historic arts institution, which has faced multiple legal challenges and criticism from Democrats, musicians and members of the Kennedy family. This language is a shift from what Kennedy Center Executive Director Matt Floca has used in recent months to describe what the board has said are necessary renovations. Floca has said the renovations would include a “total replacement of stage lifts and rigging systems” and wide-ranging electrical work and leak prevention that could be completed within two years if the facility was shut down during the renovations. He said in a court filing earlier this year that the “exterior of the Center’s main building will not be materially affected” and “the planned construction, renovation, and renewal efforts will not tear down the Center to its structural steel.” A spokesperson for the center said Tuesday that the language in the filing “describes a hypothetical scenario of what could happen if the center’s desperately needed renovation is blocked by partisan interests.” A center official had previously said the facility would not be gutted. “You’re not going to be able to stand in Georgetown and look over the river and see through the building,” the official told reporters during a tour of the facility in April. “That’s not what’s going to happen.” Mayers’ filing Monday suggested only Trump and his people could save the arts institution. The administration has “committed an enormous amount of time and energy in planning for the forthcoming renovation and restoration of this building, a task which President Trump, given his unrivaled expertise and experience in real estate and construction, and prominence as President, is uniquely qualified to accomplish,” Mayers wrote Monday in opposition to a motion from Rep. Joyce Beatty, D-Ohio, to block the administration from closing the center completely. “Even Beatty should prefer a healthy, restored Center to a decaying hulk that is doomed to inevitable destruction or collapse. The Court should allow the Board and President Trump to bring the Center back to a level of greatness far higher than it has ever had before. This would be the fitting tribute that President Kennedy so well deserves.” Beatty has claimed the closure decision was rushed and that board members weren’t presented with enough information about various scenarios before having to vote on it. The congresswoman did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the DOJ filing. She is challenging the Trump-appointed board’s renewed bid to add Trump’s name to the front of the building. A judge found the board’s earlier bid to do so was unlawful and compelled it to remove the president’s name from the building, which is supposed to be a “living memorial” to the slain president. Trump is appealing and the board voted this month to add his name back to the building in a slightly different way- going from the since-stricken “The Donald J. Trump and John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts” to “The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump.” There is a hearing scheduled on the planned name change and closure in D.C. on Thursday afternoon. The judge said in his earlier decision that only Congress has the power to rename the site.

articles.title: Trump-backed Ken Paxton unveils ‘Texas first’ datacenter plan aimed at ‘negative impact’
articles.summary: The Republican Senate candidate announced the plan with a graphic flagged as ‘Made with AI’
articles.body:
Ken Paxton , a Republican candidate for the US Senate in Texas, has unveiled plans to tackle the "negative impact" of datacenters amid a growing backlash across the political spectrum.

Paxton, endorsed by Donald Trump but facing a close contest against Democrat James Talarico, posted a "Texas first" datacenter plan on X with a graphic that the social media network flagged as "Made with AI".

Republicans have been struggling to keep up with a shift in public opinion fueled by concerns that power- and water-hungry datacenters will push up energy costs and harm the environment. Some fear the issue could prove costly in November's US midterm elections.

Related: Hakeem Jeffries defends his meeting with Trump envoy Jared Kushner

An Annenberg Public Policy Center survey last month found that 61% of Americans now oppose the building of a new datacenter in their area, an increase from 49% in March. This includes 69% of Democrats, 54% of Republicans and 53% of independents.

Last year Greg Abbott , the governor of Texas, dubbed his state the "epicenter of AI development", but on Sunday he told ABC's This Week program that tech companies "basically dug their own grave for the problem that's been caused for them and that's why they got the backlash they deserve".

On Monday his ally Paxton, currently the state attorney general in Texas, outlined a four-point plan that includes banning Chinese technology to power US datacenters, holding companies criminally liable if AI chatbots undermine children's safety and cutting red tape to ensure datacenters do not raise Texans' electricity bills.

He also pledged to support Abbott's state plan to ban new datacenters from rural neighborhoods, repeal sales tax exemptions and ensure they are adding to Texas's electricity capacity rather than taking from it.

Paxton said in a statement: "Texans deserve a fighter to lead and represent them as we address the growing presence of datacenters in Texas and stop their negative impact on our neighborhoods.

"This plan will ensure that happens while putting Texas first, protecting our culture and land, and safeguarding our families and communities. My plan will also work to ensure that datacenters are not utilized to power Al platforms that endanger our children."

The move signals an effort by Paxton, a rightwing populist who defeated the incumbent US senator John Cornyn in a Republican primary runoff , to blunt attacks on what could be a potential electoral issue. His rival Talarico has urged tighter regulations on datacenter development and an end to sweetheart tax deals for big tech companies.

Talarico accused Paxton of trying to erase his history giving datacenter tax handouts. He said in a statement: "Ken Paxton has taken nearly half a million dollars from the datacenter industry, voted to flood Texas with datacenters by giving them billions in tax handouts, and has refused to use his power as attorney general to respond to Texans' requests to block datacenter development in their communities.

"Now he's scared his ties to big datacenter companies will lose him the election, so he's making a sad attempt to reverse course by releasing a plan he literally used AI to make."

The race is tight in what is traditionally a Republican stronghold. A Fox News poll in late July showed Talarico leading 51% to 48%. The Cook Political Report describes the election as a toss-up .

Paxton is struggling to overcome a series of political scandals. He was impeached in 2023 after being accused of corruption and later acquitted in a trial in the Texas senate . He was also indicted on charges of felony securities fraud but the case was dismissed after a 2024 pretrial diversion agreement. Last year his wife of 38 years, Angela Paxton, filed for divorce " on biblical grounds ", citing adultery.

Politicians are scrambling to adjust to the backlash against AI datacenters, which consume huge quantities of electricity and water, threaten to alter the landscape of local communities, and create relatively few jobs.

Josh Shapiro, the Democratic governor of Pennsylvania, last year championed a $20bn investment by Amazon but last week signed an executive order he said imposes the "strictest guardrails in the nation". Bernie Sanders, an independent senator for Vermont, has urged big tech leaders to pause AI development.

The Axios website reported that the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned leading AI companies that voter discontent with the centers is endangering the party's chances of defending a Senate seat in Ohio.

Trump, however, remains supportive of the industry. He told Punchbowl News recently: "I saw Texas the other day sort of is against datacenters. I think it's a mistake. And I'm not taking positions, I just think it's a mistake, because there are other communities that want it. When a community wants it, it means a lot of money is going to come into that community."

articles.title: Harvard Professor Warns That AI Execs Are Pushing World Toward Factory Farming of Humans
articles.summary: "Who decided this is a way we should be living?"
articles.body:
We're racing towards a future where AI enables the "factory farming of humans," a Harvard professor warns — if tech elites get their way, at least.

In a new episode of The New York Time's "Hard Fork" podcast, the historian Jill Lepore discusses her idea of an "artificial state" that's supplanting the traditional nation state, and particular constitutional democracy, with one that erases human autonomy.

In this emerging world order, government is conducted "not by the consent of people but by machines that are making decisions," she explained on the podcast. And those machines, of course, are owned by corporations.

We aren't living in the artificial state quite yet, Lepore stresses, but it's something that's being built and realized around us. And crucially, it's also a fantasy held by certain influential elites who believe their power should supersede the actual government and the voters who decide how it's run.

"The rhetoric that comes out of this particular historical moment is really about the evanescence of modern liberal democracy, constitutional democracy," she said. The elites pushing this rhetoric aren't "interested in what the people want," she added. "Because actually, what the people want is not to have AI and not to have data centers. So that's the crisis."

Lepore explores the idea in depth in her upcoming book " The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State ." She was inspired by a simple question: in our current world where you're forced to talk to an AI to get answers, ranging from when you call in to ask about an appointment or talk to a company's support chatbot on its website, "who decided this is a way we should be living?"

The artificial state is a sort of backsliding, in which more and more of the state's functions are now being replaced by corporations that own and control our digital communications infrastructure. How we get our news, and information on elections and who to vote for, is all being mediated by these powerful groups — through technologies like the TV and radio, once, and now social media being the increasingly dominant medium.

The digital communication our lives are now structured around have a powerful isolating effect. In her 2024 piece for The New Yorker where she initially explored the idea that would later become her book, Lepore described the artificial state as the "factory farming of public life, the sorting and segmenting, the isolation and alienation, the destruction of human community."

The artificial state isn't purely driven by AI, but it's certainly being accelerated by it. People are asking ChatGPT about who to vote for , rather than talking to their neighbors, local officials, or experts. The political messages they're seeing, meanwhile, are probably in part being written with AI . Decisions at every level are being made with the assistance of thinking machines . AI is also entrenching surveillance , processing the mountains of data that is being gathered on all of us.

One nefarious aspect of the pro-AI rhetoric coming out of Silicon Valley is that it frames AI as an inevitability. But Lepore argued that this brand of fatalism is a "bogus premise," itself nestled on top of several more dubious propositions. One we hear endlessly is that regulation stifles innovation, so the government should take the handbrake off AI development. The other is that technology always advances democracy, which assures us that all of the very real threats to democracy AI poses in the present will magically sort themselves out.

Neither of those are true, Lepore says, and you have to look no further than how similar promises were made for technologies in the recent past.

"So now, the AI people come back with the same argument that was made about the internet — the personal computer, the internet, and social media," she said in the interview.

articles.title: GOP's Singer 'very prepared' to oust Dem Moskowitz in toss-up Florida race that could determine House majority
articles.summary: Scott Singer says Florida's redrawn 25th Congressional District gives Republicans a path to flip Jared Moskowitz's seat in a narrowly divided House.
articles.body: Rep. Jared Moskowitz, D-Fla., a self-described moderate, is facing political headwinds in the race for the newly-redrawn 25th Congressional District in South Florida, as Republican nominee Scott Singer sees a path to pick up a House seat in a narrowly divided Congress. "We're going to be very prepared to go flip this seat – it is a key targeted seat," Singer told Fox News Digital in an interview Monday. "This is a key district that may determine the balance of power in the House." FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: DEMOCRATS LEAD IN THE HOUSE, BUT REDISTRICTING KEEPS THE GOP IN THE GAME The race is drawing national attention and, potentially, big Democratic dollars to defend the seat in Democrats' pursuit of the majority to attack what House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries just called the "cartel" of President Donald Trump. "A lot of people in this district and beyond understand what's at stake here," Singer, former Boca Raton mayor, said. Moskowitz, currently seated in the more Democratic-friendly 23rd District, is – like Singer – Jewish and pro-Israel, but he will have to navigate a tougher Republican-friendly map and fend off the "anti-Israel wing" of the Democratic Party, according to to Singer. FLORIDA DEMOCRAT SENDS 'CONDOLENCES' TO HASAN PIKER AFTER DEFEATING DSA CHALLENGER IN FLORIDA PRIMARY "His voting record speaks volumes," Singer said. "Since he's gotten to Congress, he's been locked up with the Democrats on almost every issue." "This is not the sort of record of bipartisanship he once had. He's been much more partisan because he has to be," Singer claimed. "He has to appeal to a more far-left socialist led Democratic Party if he's going to have any influence. And that's going home to roost in November." When reached for comment, the two-term Moskowitz stressed he fought of the Democratic Socialists of America's maximum pressure campaign in his primary, while keeping $2 million cash on hand for the general election and expecting "we'll have the national resources" in the fight to keep the seat blue. "I go after my party all the time and fight within," Moskowitz, who was twice appointed to positions by Republican Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis in a show of bipartisanship, told Fox News Digital, noting Singer has been "awfully silent" on social media amid his own vocal defense against the "anti-Israel" political factions. FROM WASSERMAN SCHULTZ TO GOLDMAN, DEMOCRATIC INCUMBENTS ARE FIGHTING FOR SURVIVAL "Scott just has talking points, which is why he's the masked singer. You hear a voice behind a mask. He says things to all sorts of people, tells people what they want to hear, but nobody really knows where he stands because he never really takes positions." The heated rhetoric belies a previously tighter relationship. "Scott Singer endorsed me when I ran the first time," Moskowitz claimed. Singer's campaign has denied it was anything more than a personal call to generally express support for a fellow Jewish, pro-Israel politician. Singer, though, says he is well-positioned in the newly redrawn South Florida district, with a growing GOP voter-registration advantage and Democratic division working against the "quasi-incumbent." "People are abandoning the Democratic Party because the mainstream Democratic Party of even a few years ago has abandoned them," Singer said. "It's now a socialist-led party and it's sad for America." "That's why we need to band together and make sure independent voters understand what's at stake," he added. "We can't have people talking about communism or new Democrat-incoming members of the House saying horrific things like that they would wipe their hand on the American flag if they didn't have a napkin. That's today's Democratic Party, unfortunately, and it's not something I want to see." MOSKOWITZ REJECTS RICK SCOTT'S CLAIMS HE'S 'SCARED TO DEATH' OF SOCIALISTS, BEHOLDEN TO HASAN PIKER The race is considered to be one of 19 toss-ups in the nation (seats held by four Democrats and 15 Republicans), according to the Cook Political Report. "It's now about five points more Republican than Democrat, but even since redistricting, there are Republicans who are registering at a higher rate: People in Florida have seen the success of our state and seen the craziness other places, and they're voting more conservative," Singer said. "And we have a great opportunity to pick off disaffected Democrats who are sick with the socialist lean, especially in our community that has a large number of residents who fled communism, like my family, like wife's family did," he continued. "They understand that bringing socialism and communism into the United States is a terrible idea. That's another reason why we're optimistic about our chances to flip this must-win seat in November." DESANTIS UNDER PRESSURE AS FLORIDA REDRAW COULD TIP HOUSE BALANCE IN GOP MAP FIGHT The race also presents an unusual political dynamic: Singer and Moskowitz are both Jewish candidates competing in a district where roughly a quarter of the electorate is Jewish, one of the highest concentrations in the country. "The anti-Israel wing, which has taken root in the Democratic Party, is doing the convincing for us," Singer said. "Because we've seen a majority of House members would deny arms sales to Israel, our ally during a time of conflict. "And that's the party, where it is. We've seen three incumbents in the Democratic Party ousted in recent months solely because Israel was the key issue. "Anti-Israel is winning. It's become the mainstream of the Democratic Party. And longtime Democrats are leaving in droves. Another reason why it's going to be very hard for Democrats in this district to win with 25% Jewish population and people who understand Israel's close and long-standing alliance with the United States. We're going to pick off more of those voters." 5 TAKEAWAYS FROM FLORIDA SENATE PRIMARY: GOP SEN. ASHLEY MOODY WILL FACE DSA'S NIXON Also, while GOP-leaning, the district is still largely independent. It snakes along South Florida's Atlantic coast through portions of Palm Beach, Broward and Miami-Dade counties, encompassing communities around Delray Beach, Boca Raton, Fort Lauderdale, Hollywood and Miami Beach. "I was already running under the prior boundaries when it leaned Democratic, but I'm thrilled with the new boundaries because it runs from Miami Beach, where I was born, through Fort Lauderdale where I grew up, through Boca Raton where I served as mayor for eight years," Singer said. "I have deep ties in this district. It's my whole life. I've lived 40-plus years in this District in all three counties. My opponent doesn't live in the district. I'm not sure he's ever lived in the district. And I think those community ties help when you're trying to represent 750,000-plus people." Moskowitz lives in nearby Parkland and was born and raised in Coral Springs, which is just west of the newly drawn district, which carved those towns out. FLA DEM SEN-NOMINEE ANGIE NIXON BACKED ABOLISHING ELECTORAL COLLEGE, RANKED-CHOICE VOTING IN RESURFACED CLIPS Trump would have carried the territory by roughly nine points in 2024 after Joe Biden would have won it by about five points in 2020, showing just how the district is turning conservative and more favorable to flip. "Jewish voters don't just have to vote for a Jewish candidate who may be not terrible on Israel ... now you have a pro-Israel, Zionist candidate who's a strong Republican who will vote for the common sense solutions: We need like less regulation, lower taxes, insurance reform and more." "Are we going to continue on tax reform, secure borders, economic improvement... or are we going to go back to what the Democrats would propose, which frankly for the next two years is just impeachment? "Nothing will get done in Washington," he concluded.

articles.title: Hochul predicts Mamdani will ‘be helpful’ in her reelection bid
articles.summary: New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) said she believes New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) will give a boost to her reelection campaign. “I think he’ll be helpful,” Hochul said Monday after Politico asked about the chance of the New York City mayor stumping for her. In a recent poll, Hochul led Republican Bruce…
articles.body:
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) said she believes New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) will give a boost to her reelection campaign.

“I think he’ll be helpful,” Hochul said Monday after Politico asked about the chance of the New York City mayor stumping for her.

In a recent poll , Hochul led Republican Bruce Blakeman by 10 points in her race for a second term. The poll from Siena University found 49 percent of 811 likely voters backing Hochul, with 39 percent supporting Blakeman.

Last September, Hochul formally endorsed Mamdani in his own bid for Big Apple mayor, announcing her endorsement in a New York Times op-ed. Her endorsement of Mamdani was notable, considering Mamdani’s background as a democratic socialist and then-relative political outsider.

“The question of who will be the next mayor is one I take extremely seriously and to which I have devoted a great deal of thought,” Hochul said in her opinion piece.

In February, Mamdani endorsed Hochul for reelection , possibly helping to shore up the governor’s support among progressives.

“At its best, the Democratic Party has been a big tent not because it avoids conflict, but because it channels conflict toward progress. A party united not by conformity, but by a commitment to structural change — and to the work required to achieve it,” Mamdani wrote in an op-ed published in The Nation.

“I’ve seen a model of what that can look like in my collaboration with Governor Hochul: a relationship built on candor, a shared commitment to government that is equal parts competent and trustworthy, and results that working people can feel in their day-to-day lives,” he added.

The two New York politicians recently teamed up in proposing a new tax on property owners who have second homes in New York City worth more than $5 million. But a judge in Staten Island, N.Y., earlier this month temporarily blocked the rollout of the second-home tax.

articles.title: Second lady Usha Vance fires back at pointed jab from Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed
articles.summary: Usha Vance responded to Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed's remark that seemingly questioned whether JD Vance's Papaw would have accepted her Indian ethnicity.
articles.body: PROGRAMMING NOTE: Watch the exclusive interview with second lady Usha Vance Wednesday on "Fox & Friends," starting at 6am ET. Second lady Usha Vance responded to what critics described as a "racist" dig from Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, who appeared to question how Vice President JD Vance’s grandfather would have regarded her. The exchange began after Vance criticized El-Sayed’s views on Sharia law during a rally in Ohio, arguing the practice would be completely alien to his grandfather, whom he calls his "Papaw." "He once argued, not too long ago, that criticisms of Sharia law were rooted in White supremacy," Vance said of El-Sayed, the American-born son of Muslim Egyptian immigrants. articles.body:
Dolly Parton — a country music songwriting legend and philanthropist who captured and united fans across the generational and political spectrum — has died. The “9 to 5” star “died peacefully” at 80 on Tuesday in Nashville, Tenn., her publicity team announced.

“A rhinestone life that shone bright enough for the world to see, Dolly will forever stand as an inspiration not only through her timeless music and prolific songwriting, but also her wit, warmth, and kindness that made us all feel like family,” the statement from True Public Relations said.

In a video posted on Parton’s X account, Bryan Seaver, her nephew who served as the entertainer’s head of security, praised his aunt.

“Dolly opened doors not just for me, but for her entire family to reach the potential we didn’t even know was possible. Dolly also opened doors for generations of singers, songwriters, musicians, and dreamers from every walk of life and across every continent,” Seaver said.

“By her example, we believed that anything was possible. She never saw a door she couldn’t open, and the doors she opened made and changed history,” he added

Raised with her 11 siblings in a one-room cabin in rural Tennessee, Parton often reflected on her impoverished childhood in a “dirt poor” family.

“Mama used to sew all of our quilts and curtains for the windows, remake our clothes, and make clothes out of feed sacks or scraps,” she said .

Gifted a guitar by her uncle, Parton landed an appearance in 1967 on “The Porter Wagner Show.”

Hit after musical hit saw Parton’s career explode in the 1970’s, with chart-toppers including 1974’s “Jolene,” “Love is Like a Butterfly” and “I Will Always Love You.”

Parton married husband Carl Dean in 1966 and later translated her music fame into big screen success, starring in 1980’s “9 to 5” and penning the film’s ear-worm title song. Dean died last year.

In 1995, inspired by her father’s illiteracy, Parton launched Imagination Library. The organization mails free books to children from birth until they start school.

Parton marked a philanthropic milestone in 2018 in Washington, presenting the 100 millionth book donation from her Imagination Library to the Library of Congress’s collection.

But the visit to the nation’s capital was about the closest Parton would get to politics during her life. She repeatedly said in interviews over the years, “I don’t do politics.”

“My mother was a Democrat and my daddy was a Republican, so I’m a hypocrite,” Parton, leaning on her trademark wit, quipped in 2017.

In a 2023 song she wrote called “World on Fire,” Parton sung of “greedy politicians, present and past.”

“They wouldn’t know the truth if it bit ‘em in the ass,” she sang in her tune.

“I don’t think any of them are trying hard enough,” Parton said of lawmakers in an interview when asked about the song.

“I think often that they worry more about the party than they do about the people,” she said.

In recent years, Parton said she had turned down the Presidential Medal of Freedom due to personal reasons after it was offered multiple times by both former President Biden and President Trump.

“I couldn’t accept it because my husband was ill and then they asked me again about it and I wouldn’t travel because of the COVID,” Parton said in 2021 of the country’s highest civilian honor.

Despite the polarized political climate, Parton appeared to be universally adored.

A 2019 New York Times headline proclaimed, “Is There Anything We Can All Agree On? Yes: Dolly Parton.”

In the Parton family’s statement delivered by Seaver on Tuesday, he said his aunt lived “a rhinestone life that shone bright enough for the world to see.”

“Dolly Parton’s legacy is one of love, compassion, and resilience. With a seven-decade career, she inspired multiple generations of artists and fans with her music and an unwavering commitment to making the world a better place. Her songs will continue to resonate with people of all ages, and her philanthropic work will have a lasting impact,” Seaver said.

In a statement posted to Truth Social, Trump called her “one of the greatest Country singers, and far beyond, EVER.”

“In her honor, I am lowering the American flag throughout the United States for a one week period beginning tonight at 6:00PM. Rest in Peace, Dolly! The World loves you,” he wrote.

The Parton family asked that in lieu of flowers, donations be made to Parton’s Imagination Library .

“Dolly was a farmer, just like her daddy. He farmed the soil, she farmed songs and happiness,” Seaver said.

“Dolly called me and said she wants to rest in a beautiful bed of plush cotton because after a life wearing heavy rhinestones,” Seaver said, “she finally deserves to be comfortable and have some rest.”

articles.title: Jury sides with Louisiana Supreme Court justice in rare defamation win for public official
articles.summary: A jury sided with Louisiana Supreme Court Justice Jefferson Hughes on Monday, finding a local newspaper and two former editors defamed him in a 2019 editorial. The Iberville Parish jury awarded Hughes $300,000 in damages for an investigative editorial published in Baton Rouge-based newspaper, The Advocate, according to WWL Louisiana, a New Orleans-based CBS affiliate.…
articles.body:
A jury sided with Louisiana Supreme Court Justice Jefferson Hughes on Monday, finding a local newspaper and two former editors defamed him in a 2019 editorial.

The Iberville Parish jury awarded Hughes $300,000 in damages for an investigative editorial published in Baton Rouge-based newspaper, The Advocate, according to WWL Louisiana, a New Orleans-based CBS affiliate . The justice originally sought $10 million in damages for the piece, which highlighted a custody battle that took place 20 years prior to the editorial’s publication. The custody battle sparked an FBI probe into Hughes and his handling of the case as a Livingston Parish district judge in the late 1990s.

Hughes’s win suggests the justice was able to prove the outlet acted with “actual malice,” a legal standard of proof needed in defamation cases where a public figure is the defendant. The standard is difficult to meet , as it places the legal burden on the plaintiff to show a respondent either knew a statement was false or recklessly failed to verify it.

“We are pleased that justice was served and Jeff was able to clear his name from this unfortunate defamation,” an attorney for Hughes said following the ruling, as reported by WWL Louisiana.

The case stemmed from a joint investigation by The Advocate and WWL Louisiana with the headline, “Our Views: Before Jeff Hughes landed on Louisiana Supreme Court, he made a mockery of justice.”

The editorial stated that Hughes failed to recuse himself from an abuse-related custody case in the late 1990s. The paper went on to argue that the move was a conflict of interest, alleging he was “romantically involved” with Berkley Durbin — a lawyer for the child’s mother — during these proceedings. At the time, he was acting as a state judge.

Hughes argued this timeline was inaccurate, adding that it “took years” for The Advocate to issue a clarification.

“This editorial has been revised to clarify that the attorney Judge Jeff Hughes was dating withdrew before he made his final ruling in the Nicholson custody case,” a later editor’s note clarified.

The investigation also mentioned a 2004 FBI probe into Hughes’s potential conflict of interest in the custody case. The agency uncovered a letter the judge wrote to the child’s grandmother — who had been on the other side of the custody battle with the child’s mother — where Hughes “appeared to apologize for his conduct.”

In the note, Hughes reportedly wrote that “because of my actions, justice suffered. For this, I am deeply remorseful.”

During the last day of arguments, WWL Louisiana reported that former editorial board member Danny Heitman said he did everything he could to ensure the editorial’s accuracy.

articles.body:
The Trump administration’s plan to temporarily suspend higher tariffs on ground beef imports is still under discussion, Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said Tuesday.

“I am not privy to talk about that,” Rollins said when asked by reporters outside of the White House about the details of the decision.

“I think the conversations are still going on, and that’s Ambassador Greer who’s finalizing what exactly that looks like, and I think the president’s involved in that as well,” the secretary added, referring to U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

The secretary’s comments follow backlash among some Republicans over the proposed plan to temporarily pause “out-of-quota” tariffs on up to 300,000 metric tons of ground beef. President Trump announced the decision Friday, saying these imported products would be sold at 25 percent below market price.

Sen. Tim Sheehy (R-Mont.) said he had advised the Trump administration “against this course of action for a year,” citing concerns about negative impacts on American ranchers.

“But the reality is this action will make it more difficult for American ranchers to rebuild our herd and bring prices down for the American people,” the senator wrote on social media . “And most importantly, this will harm our ranching families who feed the nation.”

Trump lashed out at former Georgia Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (R) and Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie (R) after they challenged his plan .

The Kentucky Republican slammed the move as a “slap in the face to American cattlemen & consumers.”

“Worse than socialism! Dumping foreign beef in U.S. markets can temporarily lower prices but it won’t incentivize American farmers to raise more beef. Bring back Country Of Origin Labels & pass my PRIME Act,” he wrote in a social media post .

Greene similarly accused the administration of putting “American beef LAST and foreign beef FIRST.”

“Now they will be undercut by foreign imported beef, as they have been hit financially with high cost of fertilizer and diesel from Trump’s war with Iran,” she wrote on social media .

The Trump administration has pointed to a historically small U.S. cattle population and the New World screwworm outbreak as driving forces behind rising domestic beef prices.

Trump defended his move to reporters before boarding Air Force One on Friday, saying it was “what the voters want.” The issue of affordability has been a central theme across Republican and Democratic campaigns this midterm election cycle.

“I love the ranchers,” Trump told reporters. “They’ve done a fantastic job, but they admit that we need a little help in order to get the prices down, so that is what we’re doing.”

articles.body:
The Department of Justice (DOJ) will monitor polling sites in Charleston, S.C., on Tuesday as voters cast their ballots in the South Carolina Senate GOP runoff.

The DOJ will send four attorneys from its Civil Rights Division, one assistant U.S. attorney from South Carolina and one staffer within the office of the U.S. attorney for South Carolina to monitor polls in the Palmetto State’s largest city, the department noted in a release .

Through its monitoring efforts, the DOJ will “ensure transparency, ballot security, and compliance with federal law” in Charleston. The Voting Rights Act of 1965 allows federal observers to monitor procedures in polling places.

Voters in South Carolina on Tuesday will decide whether Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) or Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) will take the place of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) on the ballot opposite Democrat Annie Andrews in the general election.

Polls opened at 7 a.m. and will close at 7 p.m. EDT. Under state law, South Carolinians must bring a valid photo ID to cast a ballot.

Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon said the DOJ’s monitoring efforts in Charleston mark the “next stop in our ongoing effort to ensure election transparency.” The DOJ noted it has sent more than 80 monitors to 200-plus polling locations in seven states this primary season.

“We appreciate the cooperation of the State of South Carolina, the County of Charleston, and the South Carolina United States Attorney’s Office in helping make this monitoring effort an exemplary one for promoting trust,” added Dhillon, who heads the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division.

In addition to South Carolina, the DOJ has sent monitors to Arizona, Florida , Michigan, Minnesota , Virginia and Wyoming for primary races. The department will also send monitors to polling places in Massachusetts and New Hampshire, with the respective primaries in those states set for Sept. 1 and 8.

“This monitoring initiative is aimed at promoting transparency and an open flow of communication between poll observers and election monitors,” the DOJ added in Tuesday’s release, noting it enforces statutes such as the Voting Rights Act, the Americans with Disabilities Act and the Civil Rights Act.

During the 2022 primary season, the DOJ sent monitors to nine states, the department noted. Dhillon told Bloomberg last week the department plans to deploy a record 1,000 monitors for this fall’s midterms.

articles.title: Trump administration threatens to demolish Kennedy Center if renovations are blocked

articles.body:
The Trump administration has threatened to demolish the Kennedy Center if a judge determines that the renowned performing arts center cannot close for a two-year renovation.

In court filings on Monday, Justice Department attorney Brantley T. Mayers repeatedly referred to the Kennedy Center as a “decrepit” structure in dire need of renovations led by the Trump administration.

Mayers said without renovations, the site will “deteriorate further into an unsafe, decrepit structure that will be required to be taken down, with a determination to follow on what to build on the site, such as a large outdoor amphitheater overlooking the Potomac River that has been proposed, by some, for many years.”

He also argued that if President Trump is not given recognition for updating the center, it would cause “donors to flee, financial contributions to dry up, and structural rehabilitation to stop.”

“There will simply not be the expertise or funding necessary to rebuild and renovate this decimated structure. The Trump Administration is ready to go but, without it, the Kennedy Center cannot be saved,” Mayers added.

His comments echo those of the federal government against a lawsuit filed by Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), an ex officio board member of the center, who argued it was illegal to add Trump’s name to the building without explicit permission from Congress.

She said his efforts to overhaul the Kennedy Center during a two-year closure were not clearly presented to the board.

Her office did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment on the threat to demolish the building.

Earlier this year, a judge ruled that the president’s name could not legally be added to the building and ordered signage recognizing Trump to be removed.

Instead of removing the lettering on the building, it was covered with a tarp . The board, largely appointed by Trump, voted to add an inscription underneath the Kennedy Center’s name that reads: “Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump.”

The next court hearing regarding the Kennedy Center’s future is scheduled for Thursday.

articles.body:
President Trump has ordered all American flags to be flown at half-staff in memory of Dolly Parton, who died Tuesday at the age of 80 .

“Very sad to report that Dolly Parton, one of the greatest Country singers, and far beyond, EVER, has just passed away,” Trump wrote on Truth Social , adding her death is a “true loss for millions of people.”

The president added, “There has never been anyone like her, and never will. In her honor, I am lowering the American flag throughout the United States for a one week period beginning tonight at 6:00PM.”

“Rest in Peace, Dolly! The World loves you,” he concluded.

Parton, a country music legend and philanthropist whose work spanned generations, died peacefully in Nashville, Tenn., her publicity team announced.

“A rhinestone life that shone bright enough for the world to see, Dolly will forever stand as an inspiration not only through her timeless music and prolific songwriting, but also her wit, warmth, and kindness that made us all feel like family,” the statement from True Public Relations added.

Bryan Seaver, Parton’s nephew and former head of security, said his aunt “never saw a door she couldn’t open” during her life.

“The doors she opened made and changed history,” Seaver said in a video message . “My family and I have shared a lifetime of beautiful memories with Dolly, but so have you. She has always been on your television, your record player, your CD and on your phone playlist, becoming an extended part of your family whether you liked it or not.

“Our family and the team she has entrusted with her legacy will work diligently to ensure her spirit will live with us forever.”

During her storied career, Parton won 11 Grammy Awards, three Emmy Awards and an honorary humanitarian Oscar last year. She was also nominated for six Golden Globes, two Academy Awards and a Tony Award.

In 2006, she was one of five Kennedy Center honorees. Parton reportedly declined the Presidential Medal of Freedom three times — twice during Trump’s first term, citing the illness of her late husband Carl Dean and the COVID-19 pandemic, and once during former President Biden’s term.

On the latter occasion, Parton noted her preference to avoid the appearance of partisanship.

Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee (R) praised Parton on Tuesday, writing on social platform X , “Rare is the one who climbs to the pinnacle of fame, then scoffs at its allure only to retain the genuine humility that defines them.

“Dolly Parton was one of a kind, who loved people, her work, her family, and her Lord. Tennessee has forever been changed — enhanced — by her, and will never be quite the same without Dolly.”

Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) also said his state will “lower our flags” in honor of Parton.

Progressive Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) called Parton “one of the great entertainers of our era.”

“She was not only a talented musician & songwriter, but a lifelong philanthropist and advocate for literacy, education, LGBTQ+ rights, healthcare and disaster relief,” Sanders wrote on X . “Her music and humanity touched millions. She will be sorely missed.”

articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed's comparison of Sharia law to Catholic canon law during his Jesse Watters interview ignited fierce pushback from conservative commentators.
articles.body: Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed sparked controversy on social media Monday night after comparing Sharia law to Christian canon law during an interview with Fox News anchor Jesse Watters. "Getting rid of Sharia law is White supremacy?" Watters said to El-Sayed, bringing up past comments from the Michigan candidate opposing a ban on Sharia law and comparing those efforts to white supremacy. "Can you explain that one?" Sayed responded by comparing Sharia, Islamic law based on religious texts, to Catholic Church law and governance. "Nobody is trying to push Sharia law on anyone else, just like I hope nobody is trying to push Canon law on anybody else, because we live in an America where you should have the freedom of your religion," El-Sayed said. TRUMP INAUGURATION PASTOR SAYS DEARBORN CHRISTIANS 'AFRAID' TO SPEAK OUT IN MUSLIM-MAJORITY CITY The comparison sparked pushback on social media from users highlighting the differences between the two viewpoints and traditions. "He lies and says no one is trying to push Sharia (they are), and draws a false equivalency to Christian Canon law," Charlie Kirk Show Executive Producer Andrew Kolvet posted on X. "Canon law determines how Christian leaders, churches, and Christians should live, but Canon law is limited to affairs of the Church (spiritual penalties). Canon law grants great autonomy to the state." Kolvet continued, "Sharia law is MUCH more comprehensive, governing all aspects of life, and historically, and according to many contemporary Islamic clerics, dictates the affairs of the state." EL-SAYED'S AGENDA PUTS ‘PERMANENTLY’ CHANGED AMERICA ON THE LINE IN MICHIGAN SENATE RACE, GOP FIREBRAND WARNS "Sharia law is incompatible with Western Civilization," political commentator Carl Jackson posted on X. "I’m tired of El-Sayed playing the victim card in attempt to avoid legitimate scrutiny of Islam." "Yeah, it’s over for him," Fox News contributor Kaylee McGhee White posted on X. "Rogers by 6." "@AbdulElSayed doesn’t get to bloviate about sharia being a mere ‘practice’ of faith when it’s Islamic jurisprudence used to supplant western jurisprudence," conservative commentator and radio host Dana Loesch posted on X. "'Jesse, the Catholic Church requires ministers to use plant oils in sacraments with the blessings of a bishop, so why shouldn't courts allow Muslim men to have four wives?'" conservative commentator Michael Knowles posted on X. "Canon law applies to Catholics," conservative commentator Pamela Geller posted on X. "There is no compulsion is Canon law. Jewish law applies only to Jews. There is no compulsion in Jewish law. It is voluntary. The sharia is a comprehensive legal system governing every aspect of human life, and asserts authority over non-Muslims." "This was a very strange prepared defense from Abdul," GOP communicator Matt Whitlock posted on X. "I expected him to say it was out of context, not reflective of current views, etc. Instead he accepted the premise and defended promoting Sharia Law - opening that lane up to more attacks." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital reached out to the El-Sayed campaign for comment. Abdul El-Sayed previously said he felt religiously obligated to follow Sharia-compliant practices in a 2009 interview with The New York Times. "Ultimately, the question is, when I die and I stand before God and go through everything I did in my life, I don’t want to say I did it the easy way instead of the Shariah-compliant way," El-Sayed told the Times. "Not because of fear but because of obligation." Sharia law traditionally prescribed death for people who leave Islam, placed strict restrictions on what women can do and allowed child marriage. El-Sayed has spoken out against bans on Sharia law, arguing such efforts are rooted in White supremacy. "The state of Oklahoma voted in a referendum to amend the constitution to ban Shariah law. What does that mean? I don’t know. And yet the voters banned it anyway," he said in 2022. "The same exact forces that drove Native peoples from their land two centuries ago, destroyed Black Wall Street a century ago, bombed a building decades ago and tried to ban Sharia law not a decade ago, those forces are alive and well today. "The reason I wanted to go all the way back to the 1830s is because you can’t understand a Sharia ban without understanding the Trail of Tears. You can’t understand the efforts to uproot Muslim Americans without understanding the Tulsa massacre. You cannot understand the challenges we face today without understanding white supremacy." articles.title: Pritzker’s swagger stunt backfires as critics roast viral video: ‘Cringiest thing he’s ever posted’
articles.summary: Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker's black-and-white "aura-farming" video drew widespread mockery on social media, with critics targeting his weight and taxes.
articles.body: Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker showed off his swagger in a tongue-in-cheek social media video Monday, prompting a wave of mockery from critics online. The video, recorded in black and white and notching more than 1 million views, features Pritzker making a variety of model-like expressions at the camera behind a caption that reads "when you’re in an aura-farming contest and your opponent in JB." Aura-farming is a common piece of slang used to describe the taking of certain actions with the explicit goal of acquiring swag. Many social media users did not agree with Pritzker’s assessment of himself. PROGRESSIVE MINNEAPOLIS MAYOR'S VIRAL HIP-HOP MOVES SPARK 'HUMILIATION RITUAL' MOCKERY ONLINE "Only thing bigger than the ratio this tweet is getting is…well," White House deputy assistant to the president Kaelan Dorr posted in response to the video. "Pritzker is kind of a medical marvel," conservative commentator Matt Walsh wrote. "He looks gaunt and frail from Ozempic and also still morbidly obese at the exact same time. He's taking the concept of ‘skinny fat’ to places never thought possible." WHITE HOUSE FIRES BACK AFTER 'SLOB' JB PRITZKER SAYS TRUMP IS SUFFERING FROM 'DEMENTIA' Pritzker wrote the phrase "governor-maxxing" alongside his video on X. "Maxxing" as a suffix denotes that someone is doing something in a highly optimized way. "Looks-maxxing," for instance, refers to the act of taking one's appearance, physical fitness, and demeanor seriously as to maximize attractiveness. Some on social media used the governor’s phrasing to poke fun at him. Brian Costin, who is a high-level staffer at a right-of-center advocacy group in Illinois, accused Pritzker of "property-tax-maxxing," "state-and-local-tax-burden-maxxing," "cell-phone-tax-maxxing," "gas-tax-hike-maxxing," and "blaming-everyone-else-maxxing," among other things. Others focused on his weight, claiming that Pritzker was "buffet-maxxing" or "waistline-maxxing." REPUBLICANS RIP 4 BLUE STATES FOR KEEPING TAXES ON TIPS, OVERTIME AFTER TRUMP REPRIEVE "When you’re a grown nepo-kid and believe you’re as impressive as the people you’re paying say you are," Fox Business anchor David Asman said of Pritzker, whose father, Donald Pritzker, helped build the Hyatt hotel chain with his brother Jay. Pritzker has a history of making widely mocked social media posts, including his frequent attempts to spar with the president. Pritzker's office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

articles.title: Pirro hit with bar complaint over bid to indict Democrats in illegal orders video
articles.summary: A legal watchdog has filed a bar complaint against U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro, arguing she violated various standards in seeking to bring charges against six Democratic lawmakers who filmed a video noting that military members can refuse illegal orders. The complaint from the Legal Accountability Center asks the New York…
articles.body:
A legal watchdog has filed a bar complaint against U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro, arguing she violated various standards in seeking to bring charges against six Democratic lawmakers who filmed a video noting that military members can refuse illegal orders.

The complaint from the Legal Accountability Center asks the New York court system’s Grievance Committee to investigate Pirro, saying she violated rules of professional conduct.

A grand jury ultimately declined to bring charges related to the video, which shows the six lawmakers, each with military and intelligence backgrounds, speaking directly to active service members and saying, “Our laws are clear. You can refuse illegal orders.”

But the filing from the center argues Pirro’s directive to prosecutors to bring the case was “unwarranted, frivolous, and would serve merely to harass or maliciously injure the targets of her order” and that “she knew or should have known, as a government prosecutor, that her directive to seek indictments was not legally or factually supported by ‘probable cause.’”

“By directing the said AUSAs to seek meritless indictments against the Trump administration’s perceived political enemies, she thereby engaged in conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice,” the group wrote in the filing , using an abbreviation for assistant U.S. attorneys.

The video outraged President Trump, who called it “SEDITIOUS BEHAVIOR, punishable by DEATH!”

Prosecutors planned to charge the six lawmakers under a law that forbids “interference with the loyalty, morale or discipline of the U.S. Armed Forces,” though a grand jury found prosecutors did not bring sufficient evidence to justify bringing changes.

Tim Lauer, a spokesperson for Pirro, called the complaint frivolous.

“The grand jury, not the prosecutor, decides whether to indict. That is their job. Attempting to weaponize the disciplinary process against prosecutors for doing their jobs amounts to nothing more than a frivolous complaint,” he said in a statement.

Additional complaints were filed against the two prosecutors who brought the case at Pirro’s direction, made in New York and Virginia.

The Legal Accountability Center said the video was clearly protected speech and that it should have been apparent to prosecutors they had no case.

“Regarding the requirement of ‘probable cause,’ it should be evident that Ms. Pirro knew or should have known that none existed. How could it, when the comments at issue were plainly protected First Amendment speech,” they wrote.

Rep. Jason Crow (D-Colo.), one of the six lawmakers in the video, said he counted Pirro as one of Trump’s “stooges” for bringing “bogus criminal charges” against him and the others.

“They have weaponized our Justice Department, attempting to silence dissent and anyone who stands up to their lawlessness. Their efforts will not succeed because the American people are fed up with their corruption and failed policies. Accountability is coming,” he said in a statement.

articles.title: Lawmakers across the aisle pay tribute to Dolly Parton: ‘A true national treasure’
articles.summary: The death of Dolly Parton is uniting lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, with an outpouring from Democrats and Republicans alike mourning the loss of the “true national treasure.” The country music singer and songwriter died at 80 in Nashville, Tenn., Tuesday. “Dolly Parton was loved in every corner of our nation,” Senate Minority Leader…
articles.body:
The death of Dolly Parton is uniting lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, with an outpouring from Democrats and Republicans alike mourning the loss of the “true national treasure.”

The country music singer and songwriter died at 80 in Nashville, Tenn., Tuesday.

“Dolly Parton was loved in every corner of our nation,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) said in a social platform X post shortly after news of the music legend’s death broke.

“All of America is mourning this monumental loss. We love you, Dolly,” Schumer said, calling the Imagination Library founder a “force for good.”

“America has lost a true national treasure,” Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said.

“Parton’s unmistakable voice, joyful spirit, and remarkable generosity touched generations of Americans and many others around the world. From the mountains of Tennessee to stages across the globe, she never forgot where she came from, and she used her extraordinary success to lift up countless others,” Johnson said.

Parton, Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.) said, was “Americana personified!”

“World famous and self-deprecating at the same time. We will never see another like her. What a life, what an example!” Wicker said .

Rep. Steve Cohen (D-Tenn.) called the Volunteer State-born entertainer the “ greatest representative of Tennessee ever.”

“Not just from her musical talents and her philanthropy, but from her big heart and amazing grace. She made us all proud,” Cohen said.

“Rest in Peace, Dolly — you were truly an American Icon,” Sen. Ashley Moody (R-Fla.) wrote on social media . “You will be dearly missed.”

“I join every American in mourning the incredibly sad news that Dolly Parton has passed away,” Sen. Jacky Rosen (D-Nev.) said.

“Dolly was a music icon who inspired so many people and always gave back to her community, from supporting children’s literacy through her Imagination Library to helping end the COVID pandemic through her donation for vaccine research,” Rosen said .

Parton, the House Republican conference said on X , “was an American icon. A legendary artist, a generous philanthropist, and a proud daughter of Tennessee whose music and spirit touched generations of Americans.”

“This is devastating news,” Rep. Rebecca Balint (D-Vt.) said.

“Yes, Dolly was an legendary songwriter, but she was also a ray of sunshine for all and a true community servant that brought people together from all walks of life,” Balint said .

“Today, Tennessee lost one of our greatest ambassadors in Dolly Parton,” Rep. Tim Burchett (R-Tenn.) said.

“Her music inspired generations of Americans, and her philanthropic work helped provide greater access to education for countless young Tennesseans,” the congressman said.

“She represented the very best of the American Dream,” Burchett said , “and her legacy will live on for generations to come.”

articles.title: Trump mourns Dolly Parton, orders US flags lowered nationwide after country music icon dies
articles.summary: Trump ordered American flags lowered nationwide for one week in honor of Dolly Parton, calling her death "a true loss for millions of people."
articles.body: President Donald Trump ordered American flags lowered across the United States for one week Tuesday, as he mourned the death of country music icon Dolly Parton, telling the legendary singer, "The World loves you." Parton died peacefully Tuesday in Nashville, Tennessee, according to an announcement shared by her representatives. She was 80. "Very sad to report that Dolly Parton, one of the greatest Country singers, and far beyond, EVER, has just passed away," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "This is a true loss for millions of people. There has never been anyone like her, and never will." DOLLY PARTON’S ONGOING HEALTH BATTLE FORCES COUNTRY LEGEND TO MISS MAJOR DOLLYWOOD EVENT Trump then announced a presidential tribute to Parton. "In her honor, I am lowering the American flag throughout the United States for a one week period beginning tonight at 6:00PM," Trump wrote. "Rest in Peace, Dolly! The World loves you." Trump's tribute came as Parton's family and representatives remembered a woman whose influence stretched far beyond the country music stages that made her famous. "A rhinestone life that shone bright enough for the world to see, Dolly will forever stand as an inspiration not only through her timeless music and prolific songwriting, but also her wit, warmth, and kindness that made us all feel like family," the announcement said. "Dolly Parton’s legacy is one of love, compassion, and resilience." DOLLY PARTON CANCELS LAS VEGAS RESIDENCY AS HEALTH ISSUES FORCE HER TO STEP BACK FROM STAGE PERFORMANCES Parton, born Jan. 19, 1946, had a seven-decade career spanning music, songwriting, acting, writing and philanthropy. She was preceded in death by her husband of 59 years, Carl Thomas Dean, who died in 2025, as well as her mother, Avie Lee Caroline Owens, and father, Robert Lee Parton Sr., according to the announcement. DOLLY PARTON'S CALIFORNIA RETREAT WITH WIG ROOM AND DOLLYWOOD BIRDHOUSE LISTS FOR $1.95M At Parton's request, a small, private service will be held for immediate family. Fans and friends were encouraged to pay tribute on social media or through Parton's official website. In lieu of flowers, the family asked for donations to Dolly Parton's Imagination Library. TAYLOR SWIFT'S VIDEO TRIBUTE TO ALAN JACKSON DIVIDES CROWD AT COUNTRY LEGEND'S FINAL SHOW Parton's nephew and head of security, Bryan Seaver, also shared a video message following her death. Tributes quickly poured in from Tennessee and across the country. CARRIE UNDERWOOD, GARY SINISE LEAD STARS WHO'VE SHARED WHY THEY'RE PROUD TO BE AMERICANS "There are no words to adequately express the sorrow our family and indeed, all Tennesseans, feel in the loss of Dolly Parton," Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., wrote on X. "An iconic leader who loved our great state and nation. Her passing leaves a void that no one can ever fill. Dolly, we will always love you." House Republicans called Parton "an American icon" and "a national treasure," praising her as "a legendary artist, a generous philanthropist, and a proud daughter of Tennessee whose music and spirit touched generations of Americans." SEN. LINDSEY GRAHAM DEAD AT 71 AFTER 'BRIEF AND SUDDEN' ILLNESS, OFFICE SAYS Rep. Tim Burchett, R-Tenn., remembered Parton as "an incredible East Tennessean" who "never changed her accent or forgot where she came from." Texas Gov. Greg Abbott announced his state would also lower its flags in Parton's honor. "So sad to lose this legend," Abbott wrote on X. "Texas will lower our flags in her honor. God Bless Dolly." House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., said "America has lost a true national treasure," pointing to Parton's Tennessee roots, worldwide success and philanthropy. "Dolly Parton’s unmistakable voice, joyful spirit, and remarkable generosity touched generations of Americans and many others around the world," Johnson wrote. "From the mountains of Tennessee to stages across the globe, she never forgot where she came from, and she used her extraordinary success to lift up countless others." The Department of the Interior paid tribute to Parton's deep connection to her Tennessee roots and the Great Smoky Mountains. "Dolly Parton carried the music, stories and spirit of her Tennessee mountain home wherever she went," the department said. "She was a lifelong champion of the Great Smoky Mountains and proudly shared her love for them with the world." The Franklin Police Department also mourned the singer, saying her "roots and heart were always deeply connected to Tennessee." "Her songs will continue to resonate with people of all ages," the announcement said, "and her philanthropic work will have a lasting impact."
