articles.title: Live election results: Darline Graham, Ralph Norman face off in SC Senate
articles.summary: Sen. Darline Graham, a political newcomer, was slammed after being stumped by a basic foreign policy question. She faces Rep. Ralph Norman on Tuesday.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump is once again putting his credibility in Republican primaries on the line, this time for South Carolina Sen. Darline Graham in what could be his riskiest bet of the 2026 midterm primary season. Polls have closed in the Palmetto State at 7 p.m. ET in the closely watched runoff between Graham and Rep. Ralph Norman after neither won a majority in a special election earlier in August.

The president last week stopped in Myrtle Beach to campaign on behalf of the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, who South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster appointed to finish her brother's term at Trump's behest.

"This is the easiest race that I've ever seen," Trump said during the rally. "We have a great candidate."

President Trump visits Myrtle Beach to campaign for Graham, see photos

But after Trump scored an almost perfect primary endorsement record earlier this year, Republican voters have rejected his choices in gubernatorial primaries in Minnesota, Iowa and Georgia, and for House races in Florida. Graham may be vulnerable after admitting she is "not that informed on national security," in a debate with Norman.

Voters in Oklahoma are also heading to the polls in runoff races for governor and the U.S. Senate , where there is a contest to fill the seat formerly held by current Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.

08:46 PM ET, August 25 2026, James Powel

Everton Blair has defeated Marcye Scott to complete the term of her father, the late Rep. David Scott.

The Associated Press and Decision Desk HQ called the race for the former Gwinnett County Board of Education chair at 8:38 p.m. ET and 8:41 p.m. ET, respectively.

Norman is a five-term congressman, largely unknown outside the Palmetto State, who drew support from former Gov. Nikki Haley, former Gov. Mark Sanford and controversial outgoing Rep. Nancy Mace. He placed third in a Republican gubernatorial primary in June.

Norman first served in the South Carolina House of Representatives from 2005 to 2006 and again from 2009 to 2017 after working for his family's well-known commercial real estate development company, the Warren Norman Company, which was founded by his father.

He was then elected to serve the state's 5th District in Congress in 2017. The father-of-four adult kids and his wife of 51 years, Elaine Rice Norman, live in his hometown of Rock Hill, South Carolina near the North Carolina border.

08:00 PM ET, August 25 2026, James Powel

Polls closed for the Oklahoma Democratic Senate primary runoff and Republican gubernatorial runoff at 8 p.m. ET. Results are expected shortly.

The polls in Georgia's special election runoff for the U.S. House closed at 7 p.m. ET. Results are expected shortly.

07:00 PM ET, August 25 2026, James Powel

The polls for the South Carolina special Senate Republican runoff closed at 7 p.m. ET. Results are expected shortly.

Who is Darline Graham? Here's what to know

06:30 PM ET, August 25 2026, James Powel and Saman Shafiq

Darline Graham is the first woman to represent the state of South Carolina in the Senate after being appointed to the seat in the wake of her brother Lindsey Graham's death in July. Tuesday's primary will determine if she has a chance to become the first woman elected to the U.S. Senate by the state.

She grew up in Central, in the Midlands of South Carolina, with her brother and parents, who owned a pool hall, bar and restaurant.

The two faced hardship early on after their parents' deaths within a year of one another. Their mother died in 1976 of Hodgkin's lymphoma, and 15 months later, their father died of a heart attack, USA TODAY previously reported .

She was 13 years old when her father died, and Lindsey Graham raised his sister after their parents' deaths. In a 2015 interview with The New York Times , Graham described her brother as "kind of like a brother, a father and a mother rolled into one."

Graham is married to Larry Nordone, has two daughters and holds a master's degree in rehabilitation counseling.

Before actively taking part in politics, Graham worked in disability services and workforce development, USA TODAY previously reported .

Graham currently serves on the South Carolina State Workforce Development Board and is president-elect of the National Council of State Agencies for the Blind.

For nearly seven years, she also served as a commissioner of the South Carolina Commission for the Blind, where she focused on helping blind and low-vision people achieve employment, independence and economic self-sufficiency.

Who is facing off in the Oklahoma gubernatorial primary?

05:38 PM ET, August 25 2026, James Powel

Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond is set to face off against Trump-backed former state lawmaker Mike Mazzei in Tuesday's GOP gubernatorial runoff.

Each candidate got around 26% in the June primary.

Drummond saw big-name Oklahomans , including Clay Bennett, Greg Love and Barry Switzer, contribute to his campaign, while Mazzei drew financial support from term-limited Gov. Kevin Stitt and Stitt's inner circle.

The winner will face Democrat Cyndi Munson in November.

Georgia runoff to replace David Scott will test another family's legacy

A special election to replace longtime Georgia Rep. David Scott, a Democrat from the Atlanta Metro area who died in April, is being held in his district on Tuesday. Scott was the first Black chairman of the powerful House Agriculture Committee.

No candidate in the July election garnered the 50% total needed to avoid a runoff race. His daughter, Marcye Scott, and Everton Blair, the former Gwinnett County Board of Education chair, were the top two finishers in July. They advanced to the Aug. 25 runoff.

The winner will complete the final months of Scott's term but will not appear on the November ballot to win a full term. Blair previously lost a competitive House primary race for a full term to state Rep. Jasmine Clark. That primary field also included Bravo reality TV star Heavenly Kimes.

05:18 PM ET, August 25 2026, Phillip M. Bailey

Underscoring Sen. Darline Graham's importance to the administration, President Donald Trump's super PAC made a rare withdrawal from its massive campaign treasure chest on her behalf ahead of the South Carolina runoff.

Federal Election Commission records show MAGA Inc. spent roughly $830,000 on phone banking and text alerts aimed at reminding voters about the political neophyte's bid against Rep. Ralph Norman.

That last-minute expenditure is notable given that Trump's super PAC has mostly stayed out of other battleground primary contests despite sitting on a massive amount of money. It has raked in more than $403 million , mostly from billionaires and other successful business owners.

The only other time MAGA Inc. has doled out campaign cash this year was about $18,000 for Republican Clay Fuller, who won the Georgia special election to fill the seat vacated by former Rep. Majorie Taylor Greene.

"The president is going to expend substantial resources to win the midterms," James Blair, a former White House aide who now runs MAGA Inc., told former press secretary Sean Spicer in June. "He cares deeply about the party winning and anything he can do to support that he's going to do."

Poll shows Graham, Norman in virtual tie in 'toss-up' race

05:03 PM ET, August 25 2026, Terry Collins

The latest polling on the South Carolina Republican Senate runoff between Sen. Darline Graham and Rep. Ralph Norman on Aug. 25 indicates a potentially closer race than expected.

A tracking poll from the Atlanta-based Trafalgar Group shows a tie between Graham and Norman at almost 48%, only adding to the intrigue. The poll of 1,027 registered voters conducted Aug. 22-24 has a margin of error of 2.9 percentage points.

A similar poll conducted two weeks ago saw Graham ahead of Norman at 26.4% to 19.5%. That poll was taken before Graham's gaffe when she was asked whether Taiwan and the South China Sea are important U.S. national security interests during an Aug. 18 debate . Many political experts believe Graham's answer was a gaffe that exposed her political inexperience compared with the more seasoned Norman.

"I honestly have no real clue what's going to happen," Danielle Vinson , a politics and international affairs professor at Furman University, told USA TODAY. "Can (Graham) win the sentimentality vote and her loyalty to Trump carry her, or will voters want something different? This race is definitely a toss-up for sure."

Rep. Nancy Mace endorses Norman for SC Senate

04:48 PM ET, August 25 2026, Sarah D. Wire

South Carolina Rep. Nancy Mance endorsed her House colleague Tuesday over Sen. Darline Graham, who has been endorsed by President Donald Trump.

"It's been nearly twenty years since South Carolina has had an open U.S. Senate seat. Today, we don't crown a leader. We elect one," she wrote on social media . "Ralph Norman is the only candidate with a 100% conservative voting record. He is tried and true. He never backs down."

Once closely aligned with Trump, Mace has been distanced from the president over her push to release the Jeffrey Epstein files. Trump went on the endorse Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette over Mace in the 2026 South Carolina gubernatorial primary.

04:20 PM ET, August 25 2026, James Powel

Sen. Darline Graham spoke to reporters after casting her vote in Lexington, South Carolina.

She said that she was "looking forward" to the runoff results and is "confident" that she will win the nomination to take the place of late Sen. Lindsey Graham, her brother, on the Republican ballot line in November.

Her race against Rep. Ralph Northam is a test of President Trump's sway in the Republican party, especially in the wake of the ongoing U.S. war in Iran as the conflict nears its six-month mark. Recent primaries have seen some Trump-backed candidates lose in surprising upsets.

04:05 PM ET, August 25 2026, Sarah D. Wire

The Department of Justice is monitoring polls in Charleston County, South Carolina, it announced Tuesday .

The monitors include four Civil Rights Division attorneys, one South Carolina assistant U.S. attorney and one staff employee with the South Carolina U.S. Attorney's Office.

Poll monitoring is a routine responsibility of the DOJ that has occurred under Democratic and Republican administrations.

The department has sent more than 80 people to seven states and more than 200 locations to monitor polling sites during this year's primary election cycle, it said. Monitors were recently deployed to Michigan and Minnesota, for example.

04:04 PM ET, August 25 2026, Sarah D. Wire

In Oklahoma's Democratic Senate primary runoff, democratic socialist nurse N'Kiyla Jasmine Thomas and minister Jim Priest will face off, continuing the in-fighting about the future shape of the Democratic party.

Also in Georgia today, the late Rep. David Scott's daughter, Marcye Scott, and former Gwinnett County School Board Chairman Everton Blair will square off in a special election to fill the remaining months of the congressman's seat.

articles.title: Paramount’s Warner Bros. bid barrels toward antitrust trial: What to know

articles.body:
Paramount Skydance’s bid to acquire fellow entertainment giant Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD) has been mired in controversy and drew a lawsuit from critics who argue the deal is bad for the movie-making and media business.

As David Ellison, the company’s top executive and an ally of President Trump, wages a public relations and legal defense campaign advocating for the merger, a Democratic-led suit seeking to stop it appears likely headed for a jury trial in California next spring.

The case took a dramatic turn this week, when California Attorney General Rob Bonta (D) called off a planned settlement meeting over what he said were leaks orchestrated by Paramount publicizing details of previous meetings between the two sides, tainting the negotiating process.

The company and state government have been trading barbs in court and in the media for weeks, with Paramount’s top legal officer saying earlier this month the company was considering leaving its headquarters in Southern California if Bonta does not drop his lawsuit.

Here’s what to know about the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger saga and how it got to this point.

Paramount sets its eyes on unprecedented growth

Since it was purchased by Ellison’s Skydance Media, Paramount has undergone massive changes to its content strategy and business, aiming to acquire as many assets as it can and gearing up for a fight with major tech platforms in the streaming era.

The company is trying to fend off others like Amazon, Apple and Netflix, which are pouring hundreds of millions into the business of both scripted and unscripted entertainment, live sports and news.

Paramount’s news division, CBS, has been at the center of some of the company’s most sweeping changes, with Ellison tapping controversial journalist Bari Weiss to serve as the network’s top editor and overhauling its top news program, “60 Minutes.”

Many observers have seen Weiss’s appointment and the changes at “60 Minutes” as a rightward shift directed by Ellison to curry favor with Trump as he looks to grow his media empire.

The Warner Bros. Discovery transaction is seen by the company’s investors as crucial to that growth strategy, given WBD’s vast library of content and studios feeding both its linear and streaming channels. If the deal, announced in February and worth an estimated $110 billion, is allowed to clear, it would create the largest media company on earth and hand the Ellison family control of an unprecedented share of viewership in the United States and around the world.

Democrats, creatives raise antitrust concerns

This summer, a group of Democratic state attorneys general filed suit to stop the deal on antitrust grounds. A week later, a judge paused the acquisition , and then Paramount put the merger on hold in light of the suit.

The states, led by Bonta, argue that a combined Paramount-WBD entity would stifle competition in the media sector and ultimately negatively impact jobs and creative opportunities for actors, directors, writers and others in the entertainment industry.

“Film and television are not commodities; they are a principal means by which Americans encounter stories, ideas, and perspectives beyond their own experience,” the attorneys general wrote in their suit.

Democrats on Capitol Hill, meanwhile, are pushing back on the prospect that Ellison could gain more power in the mainstream media.

“Despite repeated promises to protect editorial independence, journalists inside CBS have described a newsroom increasingly bending to the Trump Administration’s political demands,” Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) wrote in a recent letter to Ellison. “Critical stories have reportedly been stalled, interviews pushed off the air, and reporters pressured to distort coverage of protests in Minneapolis and the killing of Renée Good to more closely resemble the Trump Administration’s false account.”

Raskin added CBS “pulled” a “60 Minutes” interview with Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), in which he “presented evidence that major banks facilitated Jeffrey Epstein’s illicit and illegal activities, and the reporter behind the segment was subsequently fired.”

The fear among Democrats and media watchdogs is no outlet would be more negatively impacted by the merger than Warner Bros. Discovery’s top news-gathering asset: CNN.

The cable news channel founded by the late Ted Turner has been at the center of WBD’s linear portfolio as it pitched potential buyers on acquisition.

The outlet has, however, been plagued recently by significant turnover in both its executive leadership ranks and on-air hosting roles, regularly lagging competitors in the weekly and monthly cable news viewership race.

Yet the cable channel and the future of its coverage of politics and current events remain a major point of contention around the Paramount acquisition, given Trump’s history of attacking the network and its reporters.

Trump has said he would like to see CNN operate under new ownership and praised Ellison’s efforts at CBS.

Staffers at the outlet have reportedly been unnerved by Paramount’s pursuit of the channel’s parent company, mainly with recent changes at CBS in mind.

After weeks of staying silent about the deal as criticisms grew, Ellison surprised many when he published an essay in The New York Times opinion pages defending the merger on Aug. 4. The fight, in court and in the headlines, “is not really about market share,” he wrote.

“I believe a plainer worry sits beneath the briefs and the news releases: the news. The issue is whether I can be trusted as a steward of Warner’s CNN,” he wrote. “There has been speculation about my politics, my loyalties, my intentions.”

Ellison insisted, “I do not aspire to lead these companies to bend their newsrooms to my views,” and he argued the merger was necessary for legacy media companies like his to compete with Big Tech in the years to come.

“It’s the audience — the American people — who have the final say in whether a movie succeeds or fails, whether a news organization thrives or withers and therefore whether our industry succeeds or fails,” Ellison wrote in his Times op-ed. “I want to build a company with the strength and resources to deliver for those audiences who turn to us, for the storytellers who rely on us and for the country that dreamed this all up.”

Settlement talks stall as jury trial looms

Both sides in the Paramount v. California case have telegraphed a willingness to hammer out a settlement to avoid a date in court.

But those efforts have so far been fruitless.

A meeting scheduled for Monday was scrapped after Bonta accused Paramount of leaking the details of a previous meeting to media outlets, saying the company was not acting in good faith.

“As soon as Paramount stops playing games and engages sincerely, my office is happy to meet again,” Bonta said.

Paramount, which is headquartered in California and has threatened to leave the state over the lawsuit, is denying responsibility for the leaks and has said it is prepared to defend the merger in court.

“We remain hopeful and stand ready to continue good faith discussions to resolve the Attorneys General suit and move forward with our plans for increased competition and increased output to the benefit of the talent and entertainment workers,” the company said.

If no agreement between the two sides is reached, a jury trial is preliminarily slated for early March.

articles.title: Tim Scott says candidates like El-Sayed ‘coming after our culture’
articles.summary: Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) on Monday said that candidates like Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee in Michigan’s Senate race, are “coming after our culture.” Scott told Fox News host Sean Hannity that “radical” candidates “don’t just want new policies.” “They want to change the very DNA of what it means to be American,” he continued.…
articles.body:
Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) on Monday said that candidates like Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee in Michigan’s Senate race, are “coming after our culture.”

Scott told Fox News host Sean Hannity that “radical” candidates “don’t just want new policies.”

“They want to change the very DNA of what it means to be American,” he continued. “They’re coming for our culture, Sean, and that is what makes them dangerous.”

Scott called the upcoming November midterms “the most important midterm election in our lifetime” in a face-off between “communists and socialists against what makes America great.”

El-Sayed, a progressive, appeared on Fox News Monday night in an interview with host Jesse Watters. The two clashed as Watters asked the candidate for his opinions on topics like transgender athletes and gender-affirming care, while El-Sayed spoke more about healthcare, gas prices, the Iran war and immigration.

Twice during the interview, El-Sayed requested for Watters to “just let me answer the question.”

“Can I just tell you –– you know what you didn’t ask me about? We got a president of the United States who cares more about the drapes in a ballroom that shouldn’t be built than he cares about the war he just got us into, or that he cares about the affordability crisis,” El-Sayed said toward the end of the interview.

President Trump and many Republican lawmakers have denounced the rising tide of progressive Democrats and democratic socialists winning primary elections across the country, including in New York, Ohio and Florida.

The president has painted these candidates — including El-Sayed — as “communists” and claimed that they are a “threat” to the country .

El-Sayed narrowly defeated Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) earlier this month, advancing El-Sayed to a November match-up against former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.), the GOP candidate.

A recent poll released by Susquehanna Polling & Research showed El-Sayed leading Rogers 46-39 among likely voters. The survey found that El-Sayed, backed by antiestablishment Democrats, holds an advantage over voters who view the economy as their most important issue.

But the poll also found that both candidates are viewed negatively by most voters, with 45 percent holding an unfavorable view of El-Sayed and 37 percent who said they view Rogers unfavorably.

articles.title: Pelosi: Trump’s effort to control mail-in voting ‘threatens to silence’ voters
articles.summary: Former Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) bashed a recent Supreme Court decision to lift an injunction on President Trump’s mail-in ballot plan, saying it “threatens to silence” voters. “The right to vote is the foundation of our Democracy, and the Supreme Court’s decision allowing the President to move forward with this assault on that right is…
articles.body:
Former Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) bashed a recent Supreme Court decision to lift an injunction on President Trump’s mail-in ballot plan, saying it “threatens to silence” voters.

“The right to vote is the foundation of our Democracy, and the Supreme Court’s decision allowing the President to move forward with this assault on that right is an insult to the vision of our founders,” she said on social media .

The court’s conservative justices ruled in the case that the Democratic-led coalition of states — including the District of Columbia, California, Nevada and 21 others — sued too early , without ruling on the legality of Trump’s executive order.

The decision allowed the Department of Homeland Security to proceed with plans to create “state citizenship lists” composed of all eligible voters in a state.

Pelosi stated that she believes this order is “Trump’s attempt to seize control over Americans’ ability to vote by mail” and that it “threatens to silence their voices and must be challenged.”

U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani blocked enforcement of the order, but the Supreme Court wrote in the emergency ruling that she had no authority to do so.

The court’s liberal minority said they would have kept the lower court’s hold in place, with Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, in a separate dissenting decision, calling the majority’s ruling a “ Kafkaesque nightmare .”

The executive order, signed in March, also directed the United States Postal Service to only issue mail-in ballots to people on the approved voter lists.

A separate injunction is still in place from the same lower court preventing the Postal Service from enforcing certain aspects of the executive order nationwide. It is still unclear if this case will be heard by the Supreme Court.

The Postal Service on Friday released an unpublished 95-page report , slated for an official release on Wednesday, that aligned with the executive order’s new eligibility guidelines.

The new policy gives states 60 days before the Nov. 3 midterms to notify the Postal Service if they intend to submit a list of eligible voters based on citizenship data. Only then will the Postal Service send mail-in or absentee ballots to the states’ respective residents.

articles.title: Trump admin says Kennedy Center 'to be taken down' without renovations
articles.summary: Justice Department lawyers argued that without President Donald Trump’s support for renovating the Kennedy Center the “decrepit” venue “cannot be saved.”
articles.body:
WASHINGTON – Justice Department lawyers argued that without President Donald Trump 's support for renovating the Kennedy Center – including putting his name on the building and grounds – the "decrepit, dilapidated, crumbling" venue "cannot be saved."

Congress has approved $257 million for the project. But government lawyers argued that without Trump's additional fundraising aiming for more than $100 million, the work can't be completed.

The lawyers said a board member fighting the placement of his name on the building, Rep. Joyce Beatty, D-Ohio, should prefer that to having the building destroyed.

"The crisis is so acute that, without the Trump Administration, its people, and President Trump , the Center cannot survive, either structurally or financially," government lawyers said in a filing Aug. 25 . "The bottom line is this: Even Beatty should prefer a healthy, restored Center to a decaying hulk that is doomed to inevitable destruction or collapse."

Workers remove Trump's name from Kennedy Center building

Protesters wave a US flag and hold a sign reading "you're no JFK" as workers build scaffolding near the signage for the "Donald J. Trump and John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts" in Washington, DC, on June 12, 2026. A US federal judge on June 12 rejected a bid by the board of the Kennedy Center and the Justice Department to halt the removal of President Donald Trump's name from the performing arts venue. District Judge Christopher Cooper, in a ruling last month, ordered Trump's name taken off the iconic building in the nation's capital by Friday.

U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper scheduled a hearing Aug. 27 to determine whether Trump's name should be blocked permanently from the building and grounds.

Cooper previously ordered the removal of Trump's name from the façade, after it was added during the renovation. And Cooper temporarily prevented the venue from closing during construction by ruling that the board had acted too hastily.

The board took a more deliberative process at an Aug. 13 meeting to decide to close the building for two years rather than work on renovations during partial closures over four years. The shorter schedule is projected to cost $285 million and the longer one $580 million.

"Without those efforts, the Center will deteriorate further into an unsafe, decrepit structure that will be required to be taken down, with a determination to follow on what to build on the site, such as a large outdoor amphitheater overlooking the Potomac River that has been proposed, by some, for many years," government lawyers said.

The board also voted to restore Trump's name to the façade and add it to the grounds.

The board voted to rename the building: "The John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump."

If Trump's fundraising for the project reaches $100 million, the façade would read: "The John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump Endowed by the Trump Kennedy Center Fund."

The board also voted to name the grounds beneath the venue "President Donald J. Trump Plaza."

Government lawyers contend those moves don't violate the 1964 statute creating the center named for the late president, but merely recognize Trump for his contributions.

"Instead, the inscriptions only describe President Trump's role as the one responsible for the Center's renovation and restoration," the lawyers said.

But Beatty has called the naming moves "a breathtaking act of defiance" in filing an emergency motion asking Cooper to prevent Trump from restoring his name to the building.

"It bears emphasis: On the law, the latest renaming resolution is a breathtaking act of defiance," Beatty's filing said. "Moreover, the Board has determined to add the specific term 'Trump Kennedy Center' back onto the building – a jawdropping flouting of this Court's prohibition on use of that specific term."

articles.title: Air Force officer who called for Trump impeachment criminally charged
articles.summary: An Air Force officer who twice called for President Trump’s impeachment publicly on the steps of the Capitol has been criminally charged. Air Force Maj. Jason Watson is accused of breaking multiple military laws — allegedly committing three Article 88 violations for making “contemptuous” remarks about Trump, five Article 92 violations for disobeying orders and…
articles.body:
An Air Force officer who twice called for President Trump’s impeachment publicly on the steps of the Capitol has been criminally charged.

Air Force Maj. Jason Watson is accused of breaking multiple military laws — allegedly committing three Article 88 violations for making “contemptuous” remarks about Trump, five Article 92 violations for disobeying orders and two Article 133 violations for conduct unbecoming an officer, an Air Force spokesperson confirmed to The Hill.

“Maj. Watson will continue to be held in pre-trial confinement. Airmen are afforded the right to due process, and considered innocent until proven guilty, in accordance with the Uniform Code of Military Justice,” the Air Force spokesperson told The Hill.

“To protect the integrity of the judicial process, the privacy of personnel impacted by the alleged offense(s) and the rights of the accused, additional details regarding the evidence will not be released by the Air Force at this time,” the spokesperson added.

Article 88 of the Uniform Code of Military Justice criminalizes commissioned officers’ use of “contemptuous” words against the president, vice president, Congress and other key officials.

These charges are rare , as prosecutors must prove the words were explicitly “contemptuous” — meaning insulting, rude or disdainful — rather than protected or fair criticism, making convictions difficult.

Members of the U.S. military are strictly prohibited from participating in protests, marches or political demonstrations while wearing their uniform. Peaceful demonstrations are permitted on Capitol grounds, but a protester must be accompanied by a sitting lawmaker in order to speak openly on the steps of the Capitol.

Off-duty service members may attend peaceful protests or political events as spectators, but they must wear civilian clothes and ensure their personal views are not tied to their military status.

Last month, Watson was temporarily escorted by Rep. Al Green (D-Texas) to protest on the steps of the Capitol but was swiftly arrested after the lawmaker left the site.

Green has earned national media attention for protesting against Trump during a joint session of Congress, causing the representative’s removal. The Texas lawmaker filed impeachment articles against the president on Monday.

Meanwhile, Watson has remained unabashed in his pursuit of removing Trump from executive office.

He was arrested again last week and ordered into “pretrial confinement” for his early July protest on the Capitol, with authorities detaining the major shortly after he had informed his chain of command that he would “no longer be wearing his uniform.” The week of his arrest, he had again called for the president’s impeachment in an interview with CNN’s Erin Burnett.

“When the president of the United States orders military action against foreign countries — absent an emergency scenario where American interests are under imminent dire threats, as was done with Venezuela, Cuba and Iran — that’s an unconstitutional usurpation of Congress’s authority and a violation of the War Powers Clause,” Watson originally told bystanders in July.

“These violations resulted in the deaths of 13 service members and injuries of hundreds more. For this, the president and vice president must be impeached, convicted and removed,” he added.

articles.title: Georgia redistricting battle revived after appeals court overturns federal court decision
articles.summary: The 11th Circuit said Georgia’s 2021 redistricting maps must be reevaluated under the Supreme Court’s newly clarified racial-discrimination standard.
articles.body: Georgia secured a major victory Tuesday in its long-running redistricting battle after a federal appeals court overturned a lower court ruling that the state’s 2021 maps violated the Voting Rights Act, sending the case back for a complete re-evaluation. The 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals said the lower court must determine whether there was a "strong inference" that the maps were intentionally drawn to dilute Black voting power, rather than simply finding that the maps had a discriminatory effect under permissible partisan gerrymandering. The decision follows a major Supreme Court ruling in a similar Louisiana case that significantly modified the legal framework for determining racial discrimination in redistricting. The high court said plaintiffs must provide evidence of "present-day intentional racial discrimination." "Plaintiffs must be able to show that voters are engaged in racial-bloc voting because of race, not partisan affiliation," the ruling stated. BLOCKBUSTER SUPREME COURT VOTING RIGHTS RULING IGNITES REDISTRICTING WAR ACROSS SOUTHERN STATES In 2023, a federal judge ruled that Georgia’s congressional and state legislative maps drawn after the 2020 census violated Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act and issued a permanent injunction barring Georgia from using the maps in future elections. The lower court specifically ordered the state to create additional majority-Black districts across the state Senate, state House of Representatives and U.S. congressional districts. Meanwhile, a similar redistricting battle was unfolding in Louisiana, where Robinson v. Ardoin challenged the state’s congressional map, which initially included just one majority-Black district out of six. FEDERAL JUDGE BLOCKS ALABAMA REDISTRICTING PLAN IN BLOW TO TRUMP A federal court later ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, ordering Louisiana to create a second majority-Black district after finding that the original map violated the Voting Rights Act. However, a group of non-minority voters later challenged the new map, arguing that the newly created district amounted to racial gerrymandering and violated the 14th and 15th Amendments. In the second lawsuit, Louisiana v. Callais, the Supreme Court ultimately upheld the constitutionality of Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act while clarifying how courts should evaluate claims of racial discrimination in redistricting. The ruling emphasized the need for evidence supporting a "strong inference" of intentional discrimination, rather than relying solely on the effects of a map. WHY THE SUPREME COURT GUTTED THE VOTING RIGHTS ACT AFTER SIX DECADES IN A BLOW TO BLACK POLITICIANS The decision also altered the legal framework federal courts have used for decades to evaluate racial vote-dilution claims. Established in the Supreme Court’s 1986 ruling in Thornburg v. Gingles, the Gingles framework generally did not require plaintiffs to prove that lawmakers acted with racial intent and instead focused on whether a voting system had discriminatory effects. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Georgia case will now return to the district court for reconsideration under the Supreme Court’s framework established in Louisiana v. Callais.

articles.title: Canada to place retaliatory tariffs on US goods
articles.summary: Welcome to The Hill’s Business & Economy newsletter {beacon} Business & Economy Business & Economy The Big Story Canada strikes back with retaliatory tariffs Canada announced retaliatory tariffs on hundreds of American products as high as 50 percent Tuesday, just days after the collapse of negotiations between the two countries. © Justin Tang/The Canadian…
articles.body:
Canada strikes back with retaliatory tariffs

Canada announced retaliatory tariffs on hundreds of American products as high as 50 percent Tuesday, just days after the collapse of negotiations between the two countries.

Canadian Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said Canada will match the U.S.’s tariffs “dollar for dollar, rate for rate.” The tariffs would take effect Sept. 8.

He said the 15 percent, 25 percent and 50 percent tariffs will be on $27.6 billion of imports from the U.S.

“For each product, our tariff will match the American tariff on the same type of Canadian good,” he said.

Arguably the biggest measure is Canada doubling its tariffs on U.S. steel and aluminum to 50 percent to match the 50 percent the U.S. put on Canadian steel and aluminum.

“Those tariffs will have real consequences for Canadian workers, businesses, and communities across our nation,” Champagne said of the U.S. tariffs. “Canada must respond, and today we are in a proportionate, targeted, and strategic way.”

He said the countertariffs “are designed primarily to provide protection for Canadian industries impacted by the U.S. tariffs and allow them to compete against U.S. products in the Canadian market.”

Canada released a list of over 700 items that will be targeted with tariffs ranging from live fish, frozen fish, cheese, some apparel, carpets and metal products made of steel or aluminum, among others.

The U.S.’s 50 percent tariffs went into effect on Saturday across over $20 billion of Canadian imports after negotiations collapsed late Friday.

articles.title: Report kept from residents now revealed, shows toxic levels in East Palestine
articles.summary: East Palestine residents participating in a class-action settlement say lawyers suppressed their expert’s environmental report to convince them to take the money.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Shortly after the 2023 train derailment and burning of vinyl chloride in East Palestine, Ohio, renowned exposure-warnings expert and industrial hygienist Stephen Petty tested the soil and water for residents.

Petty had been hired by class-action attorneys as their testing expert.

When the attorneys negotiated a $600 million settlement with Norfolk Southern , they did not release Petty’s results — even to their own clients.

Nexstar’s NewsNation has obtained those results and interviewed Petty.

Never-released report shows contamination, Petty says

Petty told NewsNation there are carcinogens in the soil in East Palestine and that they are “above screening levels, which means you can’t walk away from it.”

Petty said his testing data, and other data he analyzed, show dioxins and PAHs ( polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons ), some of the most carcinogenic compounds on the planet, at elevated levels.

The levels are above cancer-screening levels set by the EPA , which requires further testing and analysis.

“Somewhere between 50% and 70% of the data points, whether they be for dioxins or PAHs, exceeded screening levels” for cancer, Petty said.

“You have to do something. You have to do further analysis to see what needs to be done from a remediation standpoint. And you also have to do further analysis to determine what it means for people in that environment,” Petty said. “There is a problem there.”

Independent testing expert Scott Smith also came to test on his own. He said he found elevated levels of dioxin, too. Smith and Petty are both whistleblowers represented by the Government Accountability Project.

“It’s astounding in that it was suppressed,” he said. “Forty-nine percent of the testing exceeds the EPA cancer screening level. Seventy percent of Stephen Petty’s data and analysis shows polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons above the EPA cancer screening level.”

“It lines up exactly with my data,” he said.

Their own lawyers kept the data from them, residents say

Residents said the story they got from the attorneys in the class-action lawsuit was very different.

“Petty’s test results were always really secret,” East Palestine resident Beth Kosar said. “They said it would hurt the case.”

“They told me that in my home, basically, that the numbers didn’t support the outcome of the $600 million,” resident Linda Murphy said. “The numbers weren’t bad enough. And if they revealed them to the court, the $600 million may not even go through because the contamination levels were not bad enough. There would be no long-term health effects risks.”

Murphy shared an audio recording she said was from a meeting with the lawyers. In the recording, the speakers can be heard saying, “The data is nowhere near as bad as we thought it was going to be when this first happened.”

The speaker also said, “It’s almost unprovably bad, specifically for medical monitoring, showing that people have been exposed at a certain level so as to require 10, 20 years of diagnostic testing. Virtually unprovable for any long-term chronic future illness like cancer.”

They also said, “The chemicals did not persist long enough at quantities that will expose people over the necessary period of time to produce long-term health effects that are associated directly to this exposure.”

Austin Druckenbrod, another East Palestine resident, said he asked the lawyers directly about the tests: “I asked him when I was concerned about the testing they had, that it may not have been the truth. And he said, ‘They’re hacks. And Scott Smith doesn’t know what he’s talking about. And neither does Stephen Petty,’ And he said, ‘Don’t believe them.’”

NewsNation has reviewed text messages that appear to back up what Druckenbrod told us.

Though the attorneys didn’t share Petty’s results with residents, they did enlist a toxicologist to film a video that played for the residents.

The video was filmed by Dr. Arch “Chip” Carson, M.D., PhD., who is listed on the video as principal of Environmental Medicine Consultants. He is associated with multiple universities, including Ohio State University , the University of Cincinnati and the University of Texas School of Public Health.

In one part of the video, Dr. Carson said, “The levels that people were exposed to in the community were so small that we don’t expect any kinds of cancers or health effects to have resulted from those. There will not be any long-term health impact of chemical exposure from the derailment to community members of East Palestine.”

Petty told NewsNation, “The argument that there is nothing to see here is factually false. Multiple people saying there’s nothing to see here … are just flat out lying or are wrong.”

Mindy Bish is an attorney now representing East Palestine residents who are trying to rescind their participation in the settlement.

“Arch Carson told everyone that there was, that he would expect no cancers as a result of this exposure. No cancers. And there are cancers developing almost every week in East Palestine and someone dying of cancer almost every month,” Bish told NewsNation.

“These attorneys told them that the Stephen Petty information would not support the claims. And that is not true,” Bish said. “My first impressions when I saw Stephen Petty’s results was this is fraudulent, this is concealment, this is manipulation.”

Neither Carson nor the attorneys in the class-action settlement have responded to requests for comment from NewsNation.

Nearly 90 residents are seeking to rescind their participation in the settlement.

In part, their motion alleged “Substantial evidence of fraud and misrepresentation by class counsel, who concealed critical expert findings about health risks while inducing class members to sign personal injury releases in exchange for inadequate personal injury payments.”

In April, a judge denied their effort to reopen the settlement. They have filed an appeal alleging that class counsel’s own expert, Petty, held opinions materially adverse to the settlement that were not disclosed before opt-in.

“I believe I was manipulated,” Druckenbord said. “I believe there was fraud. And I have the future, and my future is going to rely on proving the bad actors were wrong.”

articles.title: Newsom promises new legal fight after Trump gets Supreme Court victory on mail-in voting
articles.summary: California Gov. Gavin Newsom says the state will sue again after the Supreme Court's 6-3 ruling allowed Trump's mail-in voting restrictions.
articles.body: California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced plans to sue the Trump administration over its push to restrict mail-in voting after the Supreme Court allowed the administration to enforce challenged provisions of President Donald Trump’s executive order for "election integrity" while litigation continues. The announcement sets up the next phase of the legal fight after the Supreme Court (SCOTUS) ruled 6-3 in favor of the Trump administration Monday, lifting an injunction that had blocked the order in 23 states ahead of November's midterm elections. SCOTUS stressed that its decision addressed the injunction rather than the ultimate legality of the order, leaving the door open to additional challenges. Newsom criticized the decision in a statement released by his office. JACKSON RIPS INTO SUPREME COURT COLLEAGUES' 'SERIOUS LEGAL ERROR' ON TRUMP MAIL-IN VOTING ORDER "The Supreme Court just let the Trump administration move ahead (for now) with its plan to disenfranchise voters across the country," Newsom said. "California will be suing AGAIN to block these Orwellian rules from being implemented." Newsom’s office also highlighted two election-related bills moving through the California Legislature that the governor says would protect the state’s elections from interference. According to the governor’s office, AB 282 would establish new felonies involving the seizure of ballots, election records or certified voting technology before election results are certified. SB 259 would establish criminal penalties for interfering with the delivery or return of mail-in ballots, including a felony carrying up to four years in prison in certain cases. CALIFORNIA ACCUSED OF BLOCKING FEDERAL VOTER ROLL AUDIT AS DOJ ESCALATES PROBE OF ELECTION FRAUD CLAIMS The governor’s office described the measures as an "Election Protection" package and said they build on election-related legislation Newsom signed earlier this summer. The U.S. Postal Service (USPS) and Department of Justice said they would move to implement the revised mail-ballot restrictions following Monday’s ruling. Trump’s executive order directs federal agencies to compile citizenship-based lists of eligible voters and directs the USPS to deliver mail-in ballots only to people appearing on approved lists. USPS WOULDN'T DELIVER BALLOTS IN STATES THAT REFUSE TO FORK OVER MAIL-IN VOTER INFO UNDER PROPOSED RULE In explaining its decision, the Supreme Court concluded that the challenged provision directing the Department of Homeland Security to create and distribute state citizenship lists imposed obligations on federal agencies rather than the states themselves. The court wrote: "[It] directs the Secretary of Homeland Security to take appropriate action to create and distribute State Citizenship Lists. This provision is an internal directive from the President to a subordinate. It imposes no obligations on the States, so they ‘suffer no concrete harm from’ it, and without concrete harm, there is no standing." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented. A representative for Newsom did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

articles.title: Democrats see an opening in Texas. Is it déjà vu or a breakthrough?: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: In today’s edition, Natasha Korecki breaks down the Democratic and the Republican theory of the case in the Texas Senate race.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, Natasha Korecki breaks down the Democratic and the Republican theory of the case in the Texas Senate race. Plus, we lay out what to watch for in tonight’s elections. Sign up to receive this newsletter in your inbox every weekday here. — Adam Wollner Democrats see an opening in Texas. Is it déjà vu or a breakthrough? Analysis by Natasha Korecki Texas Democrats have been here before. Their Senate candidate has shot to national prominence, raised gobs of money and is within striking distance of the Republican in the polls. In 2018, that was Beto O’Rourke, who ultimately lost narrowly to GOP Sen. Ted Cruz. Today, it’s James Talarico, who’s up against state Attorney General Ken Paxton. This time, it seems Democrats have learned their lesson about getting too bullish too soon. Even privately, they typically sum up their chances in Texas cautiously, saying it’s the best chance they’ve had in years. It’s been some 30 years since a Democrat has won statewide in Texas. At the same time, the race appears competitive enough that each party considers Texas a battleground this fall, forcing Republicans to spend in and defend in what typically is safe territory. “We have it in our top-tier states,” said Lauren French, the communications director for Senate Majority PAC, a super PAC with ties to Senate Democratic leadership. That list includes Maine, Michigan, Georgia, North Carolina, Alaska, Iowa and Ohio. Here’s what Democrats say they have going for them that could make this year different. Candidate quality: Talarico is a gifted speaker and a seminarian, who attempts to tap into his Christian faith to attract unlikely supporters. Meanwhile, Paxton brings some personal baggage to the race. He was impeached by the state House in 2023 — including 70% of the chamber’s Republicans — only to be acquitted in the state Senate. In addition, Paxton’s wife cited “biblical grounds” when she filed for divorce last year. Fundraising: Talarico has quickly catapulted to one of the top fundraisers in the party. Since 2025, he has brought in $72 million, compared to Paxton’s $16.8 million. That gives him the benefit of paying cheaper ad rates than outside groups and having plenty of runway to reserve TV air time. Environment and demographics. While President Donald Trump remains popular with the GOP base in Texas, Democrats say they see two vital groups moving away from him: Hispanic voters and independents. And here’s what Republicans say Paxton has going for him. Outside money: While Talarico has the edge in candidate fundraising, the cavalry is coming to help Paxton. Tech billionaire Elon Musk is reportedly planning to pour millions of dollars into the Texas Senate race alone. And on Thursday, Trump is slated to head a Republican National Committee fundraiser in Houston that’s aimed at benefiting the state party. Culture wars: Talarico has walked back some of the “cringey comments” he made in the past, including saying God is “nonbinary.” Expect Republicans to elevate these sort of remarks, as well as what Bernadette Breslin, the national press secretary for the National Republican Senatorial Committee, referred to as “climate alarmism.” “The problem for the Democrats excited about James Talarico is the things they like about him … make him unelectable in a Texas general election,” Breslin added. Structural advantage: It’s still Texas, which has served as a Republican stronghold for decades. “We’re feeling really confident. … Texas is one of those states that Democrats try to make really competitive,” said RNC national press secretary Natalie Baldassarre. But then reality of the state’s Republican leaning hits, she added. As for polls showing Talarico close? “As soon as the negative ads start flying, I think they’ll dip from there,” she said. Trump’s endorsement faces major tests in tonight’s primary runoffs By Ben Kamisar and Bridget Bowman Primary season may be starting to slow down, but there are still a couple of notable runoffs in South Carolina and Oklahoma tonight that will test President Donald Trump’s influence over the GOP amid a shaky August for his preferred candidates. Here are the races to watch. South Carolina Senate: Trump has expended significant political capital to boost appointed Sen. Darline Graham in this race. He appeared in the state last week for a rally, held a tele-rally last night, and his allied super PAC has spent $830,000 on texts and phone calls to voters. Graham is facing off against Rep. Ralph Norman in a primary runoff to replace her late brother on the November ballot. As Steve Kornacki notes in his “Data Dive” newsletter, Graham led 33% to 25% in the first round of voting earlier this month and finished ahead of Norman in 36 of the state’s 46 counties. But she has faced renewed scrutiny over her lack of experience in the final stretch of the campaign. Oklahoma governor: Trump also waded in here, with former state Sen. Mike Mazzei leaning heavily into the president’s endorsement as he seeks to succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Kevin Stitt. Mazzei narrowly finished second to state Attorney General Gentner Drummond in the initial June primary. Drummond has been embracing the president too: His website prominently features a photograph of him standing alongside Trump. But Trump has taken to social media in recent days to pan Drummond as a “fake Republican.” Oklahoma Senate: Even ruby red Oklahoma is hosting an ideological and generational Democratic clash. The leading vote-getter in the initial Democratic Senate primary was 31-year-old N’Kiyla Jasmine Thomas, who identifies as a democratic socialist. She’s facing 70-year-old Jim Priest, a moderate attorney and minister. Either would be a heavy underdog against Republican Rep. Kevin Hern in November. Georgia’s 13th District: There’s also a special election to serve the remainder of Rep. David Scott’s term. The race is between two Democrats: Marcye Scott, the late congressman’s daughter, and former Gwinnett County School Board Chairman Everton Blair. Scott led Blair in the preliminary primary 46% to 37%. Read more → 🎥 Tune in to the Kornacki Cam at 7 p.m. ET to watch Steve break down tonight’s results. That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.

articles.title: GOP election law expert: Many more ‘low propensity voters in Republican Party’ after Trump mail-in voting ruling
articles.summary: Election law attorney Ben Ginsberg said Monday that President Trump’s executive order imposing restrictions on mail-in voting will largely impact Republican voters. “One thing is, I think you’re going to see some blowback from Republicans in the coming weeks, because after all, Republicans are the older party and older folks like to vote by mail.…
articles.body:
Election law attorney Ben Ginsberg said Monday that President Trump’s executive order imposing restrictions on mail-in voting will largely impact Republican voters.

“One thing is, I think you’re going to see some blowback from Republicans in the coming weeks, because after all, Republicans are the older party and older folks like to vote by mail. They’re the rural party,” Ginsberg said during a Monday appearance on CNN’s “The Source.”

“And certainly vote by mail is important to people in rural areas. And thanks to Donald Trump, there are many more low propensity voters in the Republican Party,” he added.

Ginsberg has served as counsel to the Republican National Committee, National Republican Senatorial Committee, National Republican Congressional Committee and Republican Governors Association.

His Monday comments follow the Supreme Court’s decision to issue an unsigned order in which the majority determined that Democratic states’ legal challenges to Trump’s executive order overhauling mail-in voting were premature.

“The States lack standing to challenge. … It does nothing to them,” the majority opinion says .

One of the clauses in the president’s order would require states to provide a list of eligible voters to the U.S. Postal Service for distribution and prevent the agency from distributing ballots to those excluded from the list.

“Section 3 orders the Postal Service to initiate the process of proposing a rule that might bind the States in the future. It is not a proposed rule, let alone a final rule,” the majority opinion says.

“And it imposes no legal requirements on the States (or, for that matter, on anyone outside the Executive Branch),” it continues.

Trump’s order has twice been blocked by lower courts and has faced pushback from both Republicans and Democrats alike.

“Republican operatives in the states know that putting up those barriers to that part of the Republican base makes Republican turnout less likely,” Ginsburg said Monday.

“So this is kind of a flawed political strategy wrapped in a rather vocally charged policy from the president,” he added.

Despite criticism, the Trump administration moved forward with an appeal Tuesday to lift the nationwide block on the executive order restricting mail-in ballots.

articles.title: Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library says it will keep sending free books to kids. Here’s how to sign up
articles.summary: The Imagination Library will continue sending books to eligible children in Parton’s absence, a spokesperson for the Dollywood Company confirmed.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – Dolly Parton’s legacy will continue not only through her music, but through her foundation that sends free books to children in the U.S. and four other countries, regardless of their family’s financial situation.

Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library first launched in 1995 as a way to send free books to young children in Sevier County, Tennessee, where Parton grew up. It has since grown immensely, and now serves 1 in 6 children in the U.S. who are under the age of 5.

The Imagination Library will continue sending books to eligible children in Parton’s absence, a spokesperson for the Dollywood Company confirmed to Nexstar.

Families who sign up get a free, high-quality, age-appropriate book mailed to them every month.

Who qualifies for the Imagination Library?

Kids can start receiving books in the mail as soon as they’re born and until they turn 5. The program fully covers the cost of books and postage, regardless of the family’s income.

The Dolly Parton Imagination Library teams up with local partners to send books out, so you’ll need to make sure they’re operating in your area in order to start receiving them.

You can check if the program is available in your area here . If you enter your ZIP code and the Imagination Library program is operating in your district, you can sign up to receive a free, high-quality book in the mail every month. You may be directed to your county or city’s library website to complete registration.

The Dollywood Company encouraged people to donate to the Imagination Library as a way to honor the late country singer. Parton’s family announced her death Tuesday. She was 80 years old.

“When I was growing up in the hills of East Tennessee, I knew my dreams would come true. I know there are children in your community with their own dreams,” Parton once said, according to the Imagination Library website. “They dream of becoming a doctor or an inventor or a minister. Who knows, maybe there is a little girl whose dream is to be a writer and singer. The seeds of these dreams are often found in books and the seeds you help plant in your community can grow across the world.”

articles.title: El-Sayed distances from Piker amid high-stakes Senate race
articles.summary: Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is taking steps to distance his Senate campaign from far-left Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, who’s facing blowback for suggesting that American Jews’ support for Israel could make antisemitism worse. El-Sayed, who faces Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers (Mich.) this fall in a must-win Senate race, had raised the hackles of some fellow Democrats…
articles.body:
Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is taking steps to distance his Senate campaign from far-left Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, who’s facing blowback for suggesting that American Jews’ support for Israel could make antisemitism worse.

El-Sayed, who faces Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers (Mich.) this fall in a must-win Senate race, had raised the hackles of some fellow Democrats for his campaign trail appearances with Piker, who’s pushed further into the national spotlight as progressive candidates court his massive, young audience.

But Piker’s latest comments, which add to a string of controversial remarks, are putting El-Sayed on defense in the critical battleground, prompting the Democrat to stress that “nobody” outside his team speaks for the Senate campaign.

Some Democrats, however, were annoyed by the distraction in such a critical time in the race, when El-Sayed needs to be appealing to a wide swath of voters.

“It’s just off message,” Democratic strategist Steve Schale said. “Besides being reprehensible in their own right, El-Sayed has to spend valuable campaign time reacting to Piker’s incendiary comments instead of talking about how to make things cost less and other issues Michigan voters care about.

“There’s no world where Hasan Piker’s comments are anything but a net negative for any candidate trying to get 50 plus 1 in a battleground race.”

Other strategists agree, making the case that the comments could hurt him with the electorate.

“El-Sayed would rather not respond to Piker’s comments while also running against his Republican opponent,” said Basil Smikle, a Democratic strategist. “Defending his left and his right flank is dizzying for him and a potential turnoff to voters.”

In the midterm home stretch, the stakes are high for El-Sayed, who defeated moderate Rep. Haley Stevens (D) by less than a percentage point in a closely watched Democratic primary earlier this month.

The progressive’s win in purple Michigan added to a string of left-wing wins in primaries this cycle, offering a new data point for Democrats searching for the best path forward after losses in 2024.

Such proxy-war primaries, though, have spotlighted Democratic fears that more progressive candidates could be a liability in the general election — as Republicans seek to paint the party at large as too far to the left.

El-Sayed’s association with Piker had already become a hurdle in the primary , a costly contest that was dominated by issues around electability, outside spending and support for Israel. Stevens told Jewish Insider in April that Piker is “the exact opposite of someone I’d be campaigning with.” And state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, who later dropped out of the race, compared Piker to far-right influencer Nick Fuentes, an avowed antisemite.

With millions of followers on YouTube, Instagram and social platform X, Piker boasts a large online following that could give progressive candidates like El-Sayed a leg up — but experts say it could also help fuel Republicans’ rhetoric about the race.

The latest controversy comes after Piker suggested in a recent Twitch stream that if “Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone’s going to come around and take action. … Not against the state of Israel, mind you, but against American Jews.”

Rogers jumped in to condemn Piker’s comments and tie them to El-Sayed, suggesting the streamer was the Democrat’s “running mate.”

“More calls for violence coming out of the El-Sayed campaign … Here is his running mate, Hasan Piker, saying that if AMERICAN JEWS support Israel, they will be violently targeted because of it,” Rogers wrote on X.

Piker defended himself, saying on X that “this isn’t a call for violence” and that “falsely tying israel to jewish people IS increasing antisemitism.” El-Sayed also weighed in, putting distance between his campaign and Piker’s platform.

“My commitment to Jewish safety is the same as my commitment to the safety of my own daughters,” El-Sayed said in a statement on social media. “Antisemitism is a scourge, and we need to address it in all its forms. And I stand against any rhetoric that puts the community at risk.”

“But I want to be crystal clear, nobody speaks for this campaign besides me and my campaign spokespeople,” he added, suggesting that “politicians and pundits” are trying “to make this race about a Twitch streamer.”

Activist David Hogg had a similar take, saying over the weekend that the media’s focus on Piker is “kind of weird” as “the median voter knows nothing about” the streamer.

Stevens, who has rallied behind El-Sayed since losing the primary, had said earlier this month that it “certainly makes sense” for El-Sayed to “get rid” of his affiliation with Piker.

Piker’s recent comments are the latest in a history of controversial statements, including his 2019 remark that “America deserved 9/11” as blowback against U.S. military campaigns — though he’s recently said he could have better phrased the claim.

Republicans say the totality of the remarks — coupled with some of El-Sayed’s statements — are bad news for his campaign.

“This race will be determined by what the conversation is about,” Republican strategist Doug Heye said. “El-Sayed’s bizarre no-name Piker statement and really out there Fox News interview put the spotlight exactly where he doesn’t want it – on him.”

GOP strategist Brian Seitchik, said it was “politically convenient” for El-Sayed to distance himself from Piker. “Now that he’s in the general election, El-Sayed has suddenly found the courage to distance himself from proud American hater Hasan Piker,” Seitchik said. “But a change in campaign strategy doesn’t erase the record of reality that both men are enthusiastic antisemites.”

“Michigan voters will decide between a mainstream-normi like Mike Rogers or a hater with a long record of hyper troubling rhetoric about Israel and the Jewish community,” he added. “A charming delivery doesn’t make extreme views any less extreme.”

Michigan Democratic strategist Adrian Hemond said El-Sayed “needs leftists like Hasan Piker to think nicely of him” to support his apparent theory of the case that “he can remake the electorate by bringing more progressive voters” to the polls.

But Piker’s controversies don’t help El-Sayed stay in a positive light, Hemond said. He argued that more distance from Piker and a message that focuses more on the competition with Republicans than on the future for Democrats are El-Sayed’s best path forward in the race, which is critical for Democrats in their fight for Senate control.

Cook Political Report considers the race a toss-up this fall, while Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) now views the race as leaning toward Democrats, a step away from toss-up territory. The latest DDHQ polling averages signal El-Sayed and Rogers are in a dead heat, taking turns in the lead over the last two months.

If Republicans win the Michigan seat in November, though, DDHQ estimates that Republicans jump to an 86 percent chance of holding the upper chamber.

“In an environment like this, a Democrat should be running away with this race, both because the president is deeply unpopular and because Republicans basically don’t win U.S. Senate elections in Michigan,” Hemond said.

David Dulio, a political science professor at Oakland University in Michigan, suggested that El-Sayed’s distance from Piker signals he understands the high stakes and is gearing up for the general.

He pointed out that El-Sayed’s association with Piker was helpful during the primary.

“I mean, he went with Piker to Ann Arbor and East Lansing, and they packed the joints. And it doesn’t surprise me now, that he’s looking to, you know, pump the brakes a little bit. I would expect that. It’s a candidate transitioning from primary to general,” Dulio said.

“I think all the concerns are well founded because Michigan is not New York City,” he said of the fear that the far-left brand could be a riskier bet in November. “That brand of progressivism it’s going to be a tough sell in Michigan.”

Some other Democrats conceded that Piker’s comments were largely unhelpful, and as Democratic strategist Eddie Vale put it, “if those individual diversions start to add up, then it can become a problem.”

Still, Vale added, “Ultimately this election is going to be decided on [President] Trump and his cratering economy.

“So random distractions aren’t going to be fatal to anyone’s campaign in and of themselves,” he said.

articles.title: Internal watchdog finds FEMA crew violated Hatch Act by skipping homes with Trump signs
articles.summary: A Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) crew broke the law when it skipped houses with President Trump signs during Hurricane Milton recovery efforts in...
articles.body:
A Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) crew broke the law when it skipped houses with President Trump signs during Hurricane Milton recovery efforts in 2024, according to an internal government watchdog.

A new report from the Department of Homeland Security's inspector general's office determined that the crew violated the Hatch Act and FEMA policy when it skipped 11 Florida homes that indicated support for Trump, who was a candidate at the time.

It said that the incident "eroded public trust in FEMA's ability to treat everyone impartially, offer unbiased and consistent assistance, and ensure equal access to resources and tools."

The report blamed "weaknesses in FEMA's training, documentation, and oversight," saying that the agency did give crews ethics and Hatch Act training before responding to disasters.

The incident became a political flash point at the time and stoked significant GOP scrutiny of the disaster response agency. Trump eventually called for abolishing FEMA, though he later pivoted for trying to downsize it and limit aid given to states.

The Office of the Special Counsel similarly found last year that the incident in question violated the Hatch Act. A spokesperson for the inspector general's office confirmed that the new report pertains to the same incident.

The Hatch Act limits federal employees' political activities while acting in their official capacity, including barring them from using their official authority to influence election results.

Christopher Logan, FEMA's associate administrator, said that the agency no longer conducts "FEMA-led door-to-door outreach efforts."

"Staff now provide support to survivors from fixed locations determined by state and local officials through a data-informed approach," Logan wrote in an official response to the report.

He also said that after the incident, the agency gave Disaster Survivor Assistance crews mandatory Hatch Act and ethics training.

Michael Coen, who was FEMA's chief of staff during the Biden administration, said in a text message to The Hill that the report "reinforces" that the "violations were not systematic and were isolated."

"FEMA took appropriate action when the violations were briefed to senior leadership," Coen said.

The inspector general's report also notes that the office could not determine if crews skipped locations for reasons that were not allowed during other disasters because then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem did not act on FEMA's request to fund the agency's field assessment and collection tools.

The report comes after the Trump administration itself has also faced accusations of politicizing disaster aid. Politico reported earlier this year that the president had approved 23 percent of disaster funding requests from blue states and 89 percent of requests from red states.

articles.title: DOJ warns Kennedy Center could be knocked down if renovations blocked
articles.summary: The Trump administration said it may need to demolish the Kennedy Center if a plan to close the building for two years as part of a controversial renovation...
articles.body:
The Trump administration said it may need to demolish the Kennedy Center if a plan to close the building for two years as part of a controversial renovation project pushed by President Trump and the organization's board of trustees is blocked by a federal judge.

In a Tuesday court filing , the Justice Department said the center's "dangerously dilapidated, outdated, and decrepit" conditions, in addition to millions in financial losses, put the living memorial to President John F. Kennedy in a "financial and structural death spiral" that will require it to close for renovations.

"Without those efforts, the Center will deteriorate further into an unsafe, decrepit structure that will be required to be taken down, with a determination to follow on what to build on the site, such as a large outdoor amphitheater overlooking the Potomac River that has been proposed, by some, for many years," lawyers for the federal government wrote.

There are no official existing plans to tear down the almost 55-year-old performing arts center. But the warning could raise the stakes in a monthslong legal dispute over the center, which Mr. Trump and his handpicked board of trustees have sought to overhaul.

Lawyers for Democratic Rep. Joyce Beatty of Ohio, a board member who filed a lawsuit over the changes to the Kennedy Center, skewered Tuesday's filing.

"This is a not-so-subtle threat to demolish the Kennedy Center if the President doesn't get his way," said attorneys Norm Eisen and Nathaniel Zelinsky. "This is unconscionable, it is unbecoming of the Department of Justice to even put this in a filing, and we will answer in court."

The Kennedy Center's board voted earlier this month to close the center and add Mr. Trump's name to its facade, marking its second attempt to make those sweeping changes.

Less than three months earlier, U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper barred the center's closure and ordered Mr. Trump's name to be removed from the building, ruling in Beatty's favor. Construction crews removed the president's name from the facade, but the front portico of the building has been covered by a construction tarp since then, concealing most of its name.

In his May ruling, Cooper found the board was "derelict in discharging the full range of its responsibilities to the Center" by moving to close the institution, calling the decision to cease operations during renovations "ill-informed and seemingly preordained." Cooper said he was not "categorically" barring the center from closing its doors or moving forward with construction, but wanted to ensure the board followed "certain minimum requirements imposed by law."

During a mid-August meeting that Mr. Trump called into, the Kennedy Center's board approved closure plans yet again. The board also voted in favor of adding the phrase "Restored and Renovated By President Donald J. Trump" to the end of the center's formal name, the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, and moved to rename the physical site as the "President Donald J. Trump Plaza." Prior to Cooper's ruling, the board had attempted to rename the organization altogether as the Trump-Kennedy Center.

In court filings last week , the Trump administration said it will pause its latest round of planned changes to the building until Sept. 8.

Last week, Beatty once again asked the court to block the president's name from being added to the building, calling it "déjà vu all over again." Beatty's lawyers have argued that only Congress, not the Kennedy Center's board, may change the name of the building.

"In a new and breathtaking act of defiance of Congress and of this Court, Defendants have voted to return President Trump's name to the Kennedy Center's façade. This time, Trump's name will appear on the building's front portico not once, but twice," Beatty's lawyers wrote, calling the repeated additions of Mr. Trump's name to the building "a transparent effort to rename the Center in President Trump's honor."

Cooper is set to hear arguments from lawyers for Beatty on Thursday.

In response, the Justice Department defended the center's board of trustees, arguing that the resolution is "completely lawful," and accused Beatty of a "hyper-partisan effort to oppose any recognition of President Trump's contributions to the Center."

"Even Beatty should prefer a healthy, restored Center to a decaying hulk that is doomed to inevitable destruction or collapse," the Justice Department wrote. "The Court should allow the Board and President Trump to bring the Center back to a level of greatness far higher than it has ever had before. This would be the fitting tribute that President Kennedy so well deserves."

articles.title: Dem Rep Cites Natalie Harp In Brutal Takedown Of Trump's Plan To Rename Lake Ontario
articles.summary: Rep. Debbie Dingell (Mich.) couldn’t help but name-check the aide in her scorched-earth post.
articles.body:
Michigan congresswoman Debbie Dingell had a brutal takedown of Donald Trump's idea to change the name of Lake Ontario to "Lake America" ― and, yes, it included a reference to the president's devoted aide.

Trump made the suggestion Tuesday after Canada announced it was retaliating against increased tariffs from the U.S. with some tariffs of its own.

The proposed name change was deservedly ridiculed on social media, but Dingell had a snarky suggestion of her own.

"Let's just call it Lake Natalie, so we know you'll start protecting our Great Lakes," she posted on X .

Dingell was, of course, referring to Natalie Harp, a White House aide who has penned adoring letters to Trump and repeatedly declined to get a security clearance . Harp reportedly joined the president on a small plane leaving Turkey after journalists and Cabinet members were left to fly aboard Air Force One amid a security threat last month.
