articles.title: Hegseth’s Army Purges Have Undermined Military Leadership on Iran
articles.summary: The extent to which Trump’s “Secretary of War” has damaged the United States’ military capability is even worse than previously thought.
articles.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's decision to fire numerous top generals has put America's military between a rock and a hard place in its war against Iran.

The Army has been without a chief of staff since Hegseth fired General Randy George in April; he has forced out at least three senior officers that were believed to be in the running to be George's replacement, according to current and former officials that spoke with The New York Times .

All in all, Hegseth has forced out at least half a dozen senior officers, according to inside sources that spoke with the Times , who say this purge has damaged the service's expertise and has eroded its top ranks.

Those affected include General James Mingus, the Army vice chief of staff that Hegseth forced out last year with little explanation, and General David Hodne, whom Hegseth hired and then fired just eight months later.

Other axed officers include Major General William Green, General Christopher Donahue, and General James Slife, the Air Force vice chief of staff.

General CQ Brown Jr. was also fired from his position as the chairman of the Joint Chiefs in the early weeks of Donald Trump's second term, and General David Allvin retired early last fall.

Army Secretary Daniel P. Driscoll, the Army's top civilian leader, is also believed to be on his way out in the coming months, according to the Times , which reported that Driscoll has already moved out of the large family house he was renting outside Washington.

"Hollowing out the most battle-tested and most lethal, proven leaders in a time of war means troops are less safe and we're less likely to win," Representative Pat Ryan, Democrat of New York and a former Army intelligence officer, told the daily newspaper. "We're doing generational damage to the sense that the military is an apolitical trusted organization that swears an oath to the Constitution, not to a president."

Hegseth's decision to undermine top military leadership has left a definitive vacuum in the highest echelons of the Army. At the time of Hegseth's confirmation, there were 10 four-star generals on active duty. Now, there are just five—the smallest number to lead the service in years.

Meanwhile, the Army's Middle East bases have been battered by Iran's seemingly endless supply of cheap drones since late February. The conflict has so far killed at least 18 U.S. servicemembers and wounded more than 776 others. It has also taken an enormous toll on daily life in the U.S., inflaming the cost of practically everything as shipping companies contend with rising oil costs.

articles.title: Judge blocks Ohio from requiring proof of citizenship for voter registration
articles.summary: The court order is a blow to Republicans who have pushed to tighten voter identification requirements.
articles.body:
A federal judge on Tuesday blocked Ohio from requiring proof of citizenship when registering to vote at motor vehicles offices, a blow to Republicans who have pushed to tighten voter identification requirements ahead of the midterms.

In a 54-page opinion , U.S. District Judge Solomon Oliver Jr. said that Ohio's process for registering voters at the Bureau of Motor Vehicles requires residents to produce more documentation than what is required by the National Voter Registration Act, a federal law passed in 1993 that requires states under most circumstances to allow people to register to vote when applying or renewing a driver's license.

A requirement beyond a signed attestation to U.S. citizenship under penalty of perjury exceeds "the minimum amount of information necessary" required by the law to complete a voter registration, Oliver — a Clinton appointee — wrote.

Oliver's ruling also said the state's law offering voter registration to people when they are successfully approved for a license — as opposed to when they apply — also runs afoul of the NVRA, which is sometimes known as the "motor voter" law.

"To interpret this section of the NVRA otherwise would allow States to make registering to vote at the BMV more onerous, and could result in fewer voter registrations because the opportunity to apply was not proactively offered to otherwise eligible citizens," Oliver said in his opinion.

In 2025, Ohio GOP Gov. Mike DeWine signed an amended state motor voter statute that required residents to present documentary proof of U.S. citizenship to register to vote when applying for a driver's license at a motor vehicles office.

Two liberal advocacy organizations — Red Wine & Blue and Ohio Alliance for Retired Americans — filed a motion to block the statute's proof of citizenship requirement. The plaintiffs argued it "imposes an unnecessary obstacle to register to vote at Ohio's Bureau of Motor Vehicles offices in violation of the National Voter Registration Act."

The court order deals a timely win to Democrats who are vying to flip control of the battleground state where a coveted Senate seat, battleground House seats and a governorship that has been dominated by Republicans for the past 15 years are all up for grabs.

President Donald Trump and his allies have led a campaign to stiffen voter identification requirements and restrict mail-in voting nationwide ahead of the November midterms.

Trump's signature voting legislation, which he has called the SAVE America Act , would require a citizenship check. But it has stalled in the Senate, without enough support to pass before summer recess.

Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose, a Republican, said Tuesday that he "strongly disagrees" with the court order and will file an immediate appeal.

"I will vigorously defend our legal authority to safeguard our voter rolls and protect the integrity of Ohio's elections," he said, adding that "Ohio has a constitutional requirement to ensure that only U.S. citizens are voting in our elections."

articles.title: Map Shows Senate Battlegrounds Hit Hardest by Canada Tariffs
articles.summary: Canada announced retaliatory tariffs on U.S. goods Tuesday after its negotiations with Washington collapsed.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump's trade war with Canada has created a new political challenge for Republican candidates in several of the year's most closely watched Senate races.

Canada announced retaliatory tariffs on U.S. goods Tuesday after its negotiations with Washington collapsed, following the administration's decision to raise tariffs on roughly $20 billion in Canadian imports.

Economists have warned this is likely to raise costs and disrupt supply chains, especially in several competitive Senate battleground states that may decide control of the chamber in November's midterm elections.

"With this latest round of tariffs being imposed on Canada, focus will once again shift to the effects of them on Americans' wallets, especially in states like Michigan, Ohio, and Alaska, where Canada remains a pivotal trading partner," Alex Beene, a financial literacy instructor for the University of Tennessee at Martin, told Newsweek .

Democrats' path to reclaiming the Senate runs through a mix of traditional battlegrounds and Republican-held states including Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Texas, while Michigan is one of the most competitive open-seat races in the country. Maine is also one of Democrats' best pickup opportunities.

The U.S. and Canada have one of the world's largest trading relationships, supporting auto and agriculture industries as well as seafood, forestry and energy.

Many of the states with competitive Senate contests are particularly exposed because Canada is a major export market or a critical supplier of raw materials and components for their region.

Any prolonged tariff standoff could affect jobs and consumer prices right before voters head to the polls.

Senate Battleground States Most Exposed to Canada Tariffs

The Senate battleground states that are most exposed to the impact of Canada tariffs include:

"Nationally, the main issue, as is the case in most elections, comes down to one word: cost," Kevin Thompson, the CEO of 9i Capital Group and the host of the 9innings podcast, told Newsweek . "No one wants to pay more for goods and services, yet that is exactly what is happening."

Michigan: Auto Industry in the Crosshairs

Michigan is perhaps the clearest example of a state caught between economics and politics.

The state sends roughly one-third of its exports to Canada, and its automotive sector depends on supply chains that routinely cross the border multiple times before a vehicle is assembled.

Canada also targeted products tied to steel, aluminum and manufacturing in its tariff retaliation.

"We often hide behind the word 'inflation,' but that does not tell the entire story. If tariffs become the norm, prices will continue to rise as those additional costs are passed on to the end consumer in the form of higher prices," Thompson said.

The state's open Senate race is one of the nation's most competitive following the retirement of Democratic Senator Gary Peters. Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed has already sought to make tariffs a campaign issue.

"Trump is escalating a trade war with Canada for his own vanity," El-Sayed said on social media, while criticizing Republican opponent Mike Rogers.

Ohio: Manufacturing and Agriculture at Risk

Ohio exported approximately $21.8 billion worth of goods to Canada, making its northern neighbor the state's largest international trading partner, experts say.

"The reality is if residents of these states start to see the ramifications of these tariffs in the coming months, it absolutely could sway some of their votes," Beene said.

Right now, Ohio faces exposure through its manufacturing, steel, aluminum and industrial supply chains, and agricultural producers could also be affected if the retaliatory tariffs persist.

The Senate contest between Republican incumbent Jon Husted and Democrat Sherrod Brown has been viewed as one of Democrats' best opportunities in Trump country. Moving forward, tariffs could become a particularly sensitive issue in industrial communities where businesses rely on Canadian customers or imports.

Iowa: Farmer and Farm Equipment Pressure

Iowa's economy is also deeply connected to North American trade through agriculture and farm manufacturing.

The Canadian tariff retaliation has targeted products such as farm equipment and dairy-related goods, and Iowa sends a substantial amount of its exports to Canada and Mexico.

Amid the tariffs, the Senate race between Republican Representative Ashley Hinson and Democratic challenger Josh Turek has become increasingly competitive.

Few Senate candidates have been more outspoken about the tariffs than Maine Republican Senator Susan Collins.

"Imposing new tariffs on Canada is a mistake," Collins said while campaigning Monday, warning that Maine industries including lobster, blueberries and lumber could suffer.

Maine's economy is uniquely tied to Canada through forestry, seafood, tourism and agriculture.

Collins is facing one of the toughest reelection campaigns of her career against Democrat Troy Jackson as many Democrats view this race as their top pickup opportunity.

Canada is a major market for Alaska seafood products, and retaliatory tariffs targeting fish and seafood could create challenges for exporters already dealing with broader industry pressures.

Democratic former Representative Mary Peltola is currently attempting to unseat Republican Senator Dan Sullivan in one of the country's most competitive races.

This could cause Alaska to emerge as an unexpected battleground despite Trump's strong 2024 performance there, and the trade dispute could become a major talking point if seafood processors experience slowing demand.

Texas may have the largest absolute economic exposure because of its enormous trade volume, even if Canada accounts for a smaller share of the state's economy than in Maine or Michigan.

So far, the Senate race between Republican Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico has become far more competitive than many commentators expected. Several forecasters have even shifted the race toward a toss-up status as Democrats attempt to move even traditionally Republican states.

If the trade dispute begins affecting jobs or consumer prices, Democrats could argue that the tariffs are worsening economic pressures already facing households.

Canada's retaliatory tariffs are scheduled to take effect September 8, so businesses and consumers could begin feeling the impact just weeks before voters cast ballots.

With Senate control potentially coming down to a handful of races in Michigan, Ohio, Iowa, Maine, Alaska and Texas, the economic consequences of the Canada tariff battle may soon become a major campaign issue.

"The reality is that politics has become increasingly ideological. For some voters, those cost increases may not matter because the policy aligns with who or what they support. For others, however, cost will be a major concern when they go to the polls," Thompson said.

"And tariffs increase costs. That is simply Econ 101."

articles.title: What has happened in Plaid Cymru's first 100 days in power?
articles.summary: Plaid ministers say they are making good progress but the opposition say little has been achieved.
articles.body:
Plaid Cymru claimed victory in celebratory scenes on the steps of the Senedd in May, after it inflicted a heavy and historic defeat on Welsh Labour.

Since then it has been an occasionally rough ride for Rhun ap Iorwerth's minority administration.

After 100 days in charge Plaid ministers say they have laid the foundations to improve public services, and have already made a "tangible" impact in areas like childcare.

But the government failed to get over its first significant hurdle in the Senedd, when its supplementary budget was rejected by the entire Senedd opposition.

Meanwhile opposition parties claim little has changed since Plaid took charge.

Plaid Cymru formed the first non-Labour Welsh government in May, with the party six seats short of a majority of 49.

It won the election on a platform of challenging Westminster to give Wales more control over its own affairs, a promise of a major programme to boost childcare, and to cut waiting times.

The party set out a plan for the first 100 days ahead of the election, which it said showed how serious it was about governing.

It was criticised at the time as a "plan to have a plan", with the party promising to commission a number of reviews or strategies.

The Welsh government said it had made progress on a number of issues in its first few months, including extending free school meals to more secondary school pupils, a new north-south coach service, and a multi-year funding deal for farmers.

But there's a been a focus on a few big areas over the last few months.

Early on Plaid came under pressure to spell out how it would deliver its landmark childcare policy, which would see free care expanded over a four-year period.

Currently parents in work or training can get up to 30 hours a week for children aged three or four. Plaid want to expand this so at least 20 hours is available from nine months to four years old.

Opposition parties have repeatedly pressured Plaid ministers for answers as to how this will work, demanding costings and a timetable for how the expanded scheme will work - leading a minister to promise more detail .

There were questions from councils , who said the proposal faced serious challenges because of a lack of resources and staff.

The Welsh government now says that all local authorities are on track to provide 12.5 hours of free child-care to two-year-olds via the Flying Start scheme by next March.

Plaid ministers want to phase the rest of the scheme over time - but until that is spelled out the party will continue to face scrutiny over how it's achieved.

The length of time that patients have to wait in the NHS was a totemic problem faced by the previous Welsh Labour government.

Plaid Cymru was careful not to raise expectation of an immediate improvement, telling the BBC last February that the public would not expect a difference within the first 100 days .

The party promised to get waiting times "down to pre-pandemic levels" within four years. In June, the Health Minister Mabon ap Gwynfor said he would eradicate two-year waits in a matter of months .

The latest figures saw two-year waits drop slightly - by 3% to just under 4,100 pathways - but for the third month in a row the total numbers waiting for treatment has risen.

Government Efficiency Minister Dafydd Trystan Davies said the government was laying "the foundations for success to bring down waiting lists" - pointing to work on surgical hubs and a workforce plan.

Plaid is in a minority in the Senedd and the party is vulnerable to defeats if the opposition votes against it.

That happened a few times before the summer recess, including in a crucial vote on an extra £300m in spending to reduce NHS waits and expand childcare.

Labour had demanded £100m extra to be spent on children with additional learning needs - and the two sides had failed to come to an agreement.

It was the first time a Welsh government has lost a vote on a supplementary budget - which is in addition to the main budget exercise that happens in the autumn.

Laura McAllister, professor of politics at Cardiff University, said she thought the government had been a little naive.

"If you're in that position of being a minority government, transactional relationships and goodwill between the parties is absolutely fundamental."

Since then, Welsh Labour leader Ken Skates has indicated that he does want a budget deal with Plaid .

The Plaid government faced its first major incident over the summer as a devolved government when a number of wildfires broke out in Wales.

The Welsh government came under scrutiny for its crisis management, because unlike the police, fire services are devolved in Wales.

There was criticism from Reform Wales about the time taken in to bring in the army and aerial support .

A minister said lessons needed to be learned with wildfires more likely in the future due to climate change.

Plaid Cymru wants powers over policing and justice, rail infrastructure and the Crown Estate to be devolved from Westminster to Cardiff.

It promised negotiations with Westminster to do that, but turmoil in London has made making the case tricky.

Ap Iorwerth tried and failed to get a meeting with the previous prime minister, Sir Keir Starmer, although the man now in charge, Andy Burnham, held his first face-to-face meeting with the first minister in July .

Burnham has promised to put devolution front and centre of his government.

But his Welsh Secretary, Stephen Kinnock, has said he is not yet "entirely convinced" by the case for more responsibilities for the Welsh government.

Some at Collier's Adventure Farm in Nelson, Caerphilly, were willing to give the Plaid Cymru government time before rushing to judgement.

Raydean Thomas said: "I think they're finding their feet at the moment. Nothing that they've done has been wrong as far as I can say. I think they're thinking of things in the right way."

Faye Dalgleish-McGee said: "People do rush to have an opinion a bit too quickly - let them get settled in before we start complaining."

Meanwhile, Trish Garner said it was important to wait to see what their plans are.

"But I don't hear an awful lot about what they're going to do and that's my feeling," she added.

Michael Davies said his life had not changed since Plaid had got into power, and that politics was the "same old story" with successive governments blaming each other.

"[They say] it's going to take us x amount of years to put it right and then nothing seems to happen."

Julie Jones, who was also at the coffee morning, said it was too soon to judge ap Iorwerth, but that "he came in all guns blazing".

Dafydd Trystan Davies said that "the initial work has been completed on the 96 actions" in the party's 100-day plan.

He said that in some areas the administration had "put the foundations for success in place".

"But in others, we've made tangible real progress that people will be able to feel already," he said.

The first minister is on leave until the end of the week and was unavailable for interviews ahead of the completion of 100 days in government.

Asked by BBC Wales whether that meant the government was playing down the milestone, Davies said it was him that was responsible for 100-day programme and that ap Iorwerth will issue a "progress report" next week.

Reform accused Plaid of focusing too much on "reviews, committees and plans".

Dan Thomas, Reform's Welsh leader, told BBC Wales that things have "just got worse" since Plaid won the election, with waiting lists having "gone up".

"The first minister said during the election campaign that two-year waits would be eradicated within a matter of months. We're now three months into a Plaid government and we're nowhere near seeing those waits being eradicated."

Ken Skates, leader of Welsh Labour, said there was "quite a contrast" between Plaid Cymru's first 100 days and the start of Andy Burnham's premiership.

"We've seen plans and processes here, discussion, a lot of talk, very little action. In contrast with Andy Burnham, we've seen some really, really big interventions that are going to make a difference to people's lives."

Darren Millar MS, Leader of the Welsh Conservatives in the Senedd, said: "Plaid's first 100 days have been a disappointing series of missed opportunities to turn the page on 27 years of Labour rule in Wales."

articles.title: Trump Insider Predicts Brutal Loss for His Chosen Candidate
articles.summary: Donald Trump’s former White House press secretary has predicted that the president’s choice for Senate in South Carolina will lose Tuesday night’s Republican...
articles.body:
Donald Trump's former White House press secretary has predicted that the president's choice for Senate in South Carolina will lose Tuesday night's Republican primary.

Sean Spicer, who served in the Trump administration for the first six months of the president's first term, said on The Huddle that Rep. Ralph Norman "is going to come out ahead" of Sen. Darline Graham. Trump, 80, endorsed Graham, who is running for a full term after being appointed to replace her brother following his death in July. Even with the president's involvement, polls show the race is close.

Spicer, citing a Trafalgar poll showing Graham, 62, and Norman, 73, essentially tied at just under 48 percent, commented that it was not a good sign that Graham hadn't surpassed 50 percent, considering all that has been done for her campaign.

"They've thrown everything at it. There's a story in Politico this morning that they've spent almost a million dollars on texts, on 'get out the vote,'" Spicer, 54, said. South Carolina Sen. Tim Scott appeared on Fox News' Hannity on Monday night to try to lock up support, Spicer mentioned, and Trump flew to South Carolina last week and held a rally with Graham.

"They've thrown the kitchen sink, the trash compactor, the faucets—they've thrown everything at this race," Spicer said. "I will say, I think Ralph Norman's going to come out ahead tonight."

If that's the case, it may be due in part to some hiccups in Graham's campaign.

When asked during a debate against Norman last Tuesday whether Taiwan and the South China Sea were national security issues for the U.S., Graham said, "I'm just going to be honest here... I'm not that informed on national security."

She added: "I'm not a polished politician up here. National security is not my thing, not my area of expertise, but I support the military."

Then over the weekend, Graham took issue with a constituent recording their conversation at a campaign event, even though South Carolina is a one-party consent state.

"Is your phone recording this?" Darline asked the woman, who responded, "Yes, because, I mean, this is a political event. There's always phones recording. So, you're a politician. You know the drill."

Darline answered, "It kind of does bother me that you're recording me—I'm being honest—without my permission." A staffer then ended the conversation between the two women.

And on the eve of Tuesday's primary, Graham refused to acknowledge that Trump lost the 2020 election.

"Senator, you just mentioned that you agree with your brother on everything except for one matter, that being illegal immigration; you'd go farther than him on that," MS NOW congressional reporter Mychael Schnell told Graham. "That being said, I'm curious, do you agree with him about the 2020 election, that Joe Biden was certified the winner of that election, was lawfully elected, and that you would've voted to certify the election as your brother did?"

Graham skirted the question, saying, "I think our election system is broken." She ignored a follow-up question.
